docs.title: Cadwyn
docs.text: Production-ready community-driven modern Stripe-like API versioning in FastAPI

docs.title: Who is this for?
docs.text:
Cadwyn allows you to maintain the implementation just for your newest API version and get all the older versions generated automatically. You keep API backward compatibility encapsulated in small and independent "version change" modules while your business logic stays simple and knows nothing about versioning.

This approach may be useful if you want to:

  1. Support many API versions for a long time
  2. Have features and bugfixes automatically backported to older API versions

Whether you are a newbie in API versioning, a pro looking for a sophisticated tool, an experimenter looking to build a similar framework, or even someone who just wants to learn about all approaches to API versioning -- Cadwyn has the functionality, theory, and documentation to cover all the mentioned use cases.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text: It is recommended to read the quickstart tutorial first to get your feet wet with Cadwyn's approach

docs.title: Concepts
docs.text:
This section covers the entirety of the features and their rationale in Cadwyn. To begin with, here are the reasons for using Cadwyn at all.

Cadwyn aims to be the most accurate and sophisticated API versioning framework out there. First of all, Cadwyn users maintain no duplicated code. Usually, API versioning requires duplicating and maintaining at least some layer of your application. It could be the database, business logic, schemas, or endpoints. With Cadwyn you avoid duplicating any of that. Internally, Cadwyn duplicates endpoints and schemas at runtime but none of it becomes your tech debt, none of it becomes your code to support. If you test rigorously, only a small subset of your tests needs to be duplicated when existing functionality changes between versions.

You define your database, business logic, routes, and schemas only once. Then, whenever you release a new API version, you use Cadwyn's version change DSL to describe how to convert your app to the previous version. So your business logic and database remain intact and always represent the latest version while the version changes ensure that your clients can continue using the previous versions without updating their code.

This allows you to maintain hundreds of versions effortlessly, unlike other API versioning approaches.

docs.title: API version parameter
docs.text: Cadwyn adds another routing layer to FastAPI by default: by a version parameter. This means that before FastAPI selects the correct route for the request, Cadwyn decides which version of the route will be used based on the version parameter. Feel free to look at the example app with URL path version prefixes and arbitrary strings as versions here.

docs.title: API version location
docs.text:
A version parameter can be passed in two different ways:

  • as a custom header
  • as a URL path parameter

Cadwyn uses the following defaults:

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle

app = Cadwyn(
    api_version_location="custom_header",
    api_version_parameter_name="x-api-version",
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2022-01-02")),
)

but you can change the header name if you want to:

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle

app = Cadwyn(
    api_version_location="custom_header",
    api_version_parameter_name="MY-GREAT-HEADER",
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2022-01-02")),
)

or you can use a path parameter:

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle

app = Cadwyn(
    api_version_location="path",
    api_version_parameter_name="api_version",
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2022-01-02")),
)

With a path parameter, add it to the paths of your versioned routes, e.g. @router.get("/{api_version}/users").

docs.title: API version format
docs.text:
A version parameter can be formatted in two different ways:

  • as an ISO date
  • as an arbitrary string

Cadwyn uses the following default:

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle

app = Cadwyn(
    api_version_format="date",
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2022-01-02")),
)

In the example above only dates are accepted as valid versions.

You can also use an arbitrary string:

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle

app = Cadwyn(
    api_version_format="string",
    versions=VersionBundle(
        Version("v2"),
        Version("anything_can_be_a_version"),
        Version("v1"),
    ),
)

In the example above any arbitrary string is accepted as a valid version. Cadwyn does not sort them, Cadwyn assumes that their actual order matches the order of the versions in the VersionBundle.

docs.title: API version waterfalling
docs.text:
For historical reasons, date-based routing also supports waterfalling the requests to the closest earlier version of the API if the request date parameter does not match any of the versions exactly.

If the app has two versions: 2022-01-02 and 2022-01-05, and the request date parameter is 2022-01-03, then the request will be routed to the 2022-01-02 version, as it is the closest version, but lower than the request date parameter.

An exact match is always preferred to a partial match and a request is never matched to the higher-versioned route.

The routing is implemented like this because Cadwyn was born in a microservice architecture and it is extremely convenient to have waterfalling there. Assume that you have two Cadwyn services: Payables and Receivables, each defining its own API versions. Payables service might have ten versions while Receivables service might have only two versions because it did not need as many breaking changes. If a client requests a version that does not exist in Receivables, Cadwyn will waterfall to some earlier version, making Receivables behavior consistent even if API keeps getting new versions.

docs.title: Requests without an API version
docs.text: Cadwyn routes versioned endpoints by the API version, so a request without it gets a 404. That's why the OpenAPI of each version documents the version header as required unless you set a default API version. Some clients cannot send the version header. For example, Swagger UI's "Authorize" button for OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl=...) sends the token request to tokenUrl without any custom headers. You have two options for such endpoints.

docs.title: Keep the endpoint unversioned
docs.text:
Define the endpoint on a regular fastapi.APIRouter and include it with app.include_router(), either before or after generate_and_include_versioned_routers(). Cadwyn does not version such routes:

from typing import Annotated

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle, VersionedAPIRouter
from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="/token")

# A regular FastAPI router: Cadwyn does not version its routes
auth_router = APIRouter()


@auth_router.post("/token")
async def login(
    form_data: Annotated[OAuth2PasswordRequestForm, Depends()],
):
    # Check the credentials and issue a real token here
    return {"access_token": form_data.username, "token_type": "bearer"}


router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.get("/users/me")
async def read_current_user(token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)]):
    return {"token": token}


app = Cadwyn(versions=VersionBundle(Version("2000-01-01")))
app.include_router(auth_router)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

Unversioned routes are only available to requests without the version header, so all clients have to call this endpoint without it. Cadwyn does not migrate unversioned endpoints, so if you ever change this endpoint, keep it compatible with your older clients and cover that with tests.

docs.title: Set a default API version
docs.text:
Pass api_version_default_value to Cadwyn to route the requests without the version header to a specific version:

from typing import Annotated

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle, VersionedAPIRouter
from fastapi import Depends
from fastapi.security import OAuth2PasswordBearer, OAuth2PasswordRequestForm

oauth2_scheme = OAuth2PasswordBearer(tokenUrl="/token")
router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.post("/token")
async def login(
    form_data: Annotated[OAuth2PasswordRequestForm, Depends()],
):
    # Check the credentials and issue a real token here
    return {"access_token": form_data.username, "token_type": "bearer"}


@router.get("/users/me")
async def read_current_user(token: Annotated[str, Depends(oauth2_scheme)]):
    return {"token": token}


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2000-01-01")),
    # Requests without the version header get this version
    api_version_default_value="2000-01-01",
)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

Note that this applies to every request without the version header, not only to the token endpoint. api_version_default_value can also be an async function that takes the Request and returns the version.

docs.title: WebSocket connections
docs.text:
WebSocket routes included with generate_and_include_versioned_routers() select their version from the configured header or path parameter. Date versions use the closest earlier version when there is no exact match. Header versioning also supports a constant api_version_default_value.

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle, VersionedAPIRouter
from fastapi import WebSocket

versions = VersionBundle(Version("2024-02-01"), Version("2024-01-01"))
app = Cadwyn(versions=versions)
router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.websocket("/ws")
async def websocket_endpoint(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()
    await websocket.send_json({"version": versions.api_version_var.get()})
    await websocket.close()


app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

The selected version is available in versions.api_version_var before dependencies run, throughout the connection and dependency cleanup. Cadwyn restores the previous context when the connection ends. Missing, invalid, and unmatched versions close the connection before acceptance with code 1008 and an API version reason. A callable api_version_default_value requires an HTTP Request: for WebSockets, send the version explicitly or use a constant default.

Routes included with app.include_router() keep working as unversioned WebSockets, even when a version header or default is present. A version preselected in api_version_var retains its routing behavior. WebSockets stay out of OpenAPI. See WebSocket endpoint migrations for changing their routes and dependencies between versions.

docs.title: API version parameter title and description
docs.text:
You can pass a title and/or a description to the Cadwyn() constructor. It is equivalent to passing title and description to fastapi.Path() or fastapi.Header() constructors.

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle

app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2022-01-02")),
    api_version_title="My Great API version parameter",
    api_version_description="Description of my great API version parameter",
)

docs.title: API version context variables
docs.text:
Cadwyn automatically converts your data to the correct version and has "version checks" when dealing with side effects as described in the section above. It can only do so using a special context variable that stores the current API version.

You can also pass a different compatible contextvar to your cadwyn.VersionBundle() constructor.

docs.title: Beware of data versioning
docs.text:
Often you may want to introduce a breaking change when one of the following is true:

  • Old data cannot be automatically converted to the structure of the new response
  • New response cannot be automatically migrated to an older response
  • Old request cannot be automatically converted to the HEAD request

This means that you are not versioning your API, you are versioning your data. Such an issue cannot be solved using an API versioning framework. It also makes it incredibly hard to version as you now cannot guarantee compatibility between versions. Avoid this at all costs — all your API versions must be compatible between each other. Data versioning is not a result of a complicated use case, it is a result of errors when devising a new version. I have yet to see a single case where data versioning is the right way to solve an API versioning issue.

docs.title: CLI
docs.text:
Cadwyn has an optional CLI that can be installed with uv add 'cadwyn[standard]'.

Its main purpose is to render generated schemas.

You can check the current version of Cadwyn using the CLI:

cadwyn --version

docs.title: Endpoint migrations
docs.text: Note that the endpoint(...) constructor contains a second argument that describes the methods of the endpoints you would like to edit. If you have two routes for a single endpoint and you include both of their methods in the instructions, both of them will be changed.

docs.title: Defining endpoints that did not exist for new versions
docs.text:
If you have an endpoint in an old version but want to delete it in a new version, define it as usual with all your other endpoints but mark it as deleted...

@router.only_exists_in_older_versions
@router.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def my_old_endpoint(): ...

and then define it as existing in one of the older versions:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, endpoint


class RemoveGetUserByIdEndpoint(VersionChange):
    """The 'GET /users/{user_id}' endpoint has been removed because user
    profiles are now retrieved through the users collection.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        endpoint("/users/{user_id}", ["GET"]).existed,
    )

docs.title: Defining endpoints that did not exist for old versions
docs.text:
If you have an endpoint in a new version that should not exist in older versions, define it as usual and then mark it as "nonexistent" in old versions. Note that this approach is not recommended for adding new endpoints.

from cadwyn import VersionChange, endpoint


class AddGetCompanyByIdEndpoint(VersionChange):
    """Clients can now retrieve an individual company with
    'GET /companies/{company_id}' instead of filtering the company list.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        endpoint("/companies/{company_id}", ["GET"]).didnt_exist,
    )

docs.title: Changing endpoint attributes
docs.text:
If you want to change an endpoint attribute (like description) in a new version, you can return its value in all older versions like this:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, endpoint


class ChangeGetUserByIdEndpointDescription(VersionChange):
    """The 'GET /users/{user_id}' documentation now clarifies the returned
    user data so clients can interpret the response correctly.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        endpoint("/users/{user_id}", ["GET"]).had(
            description="My old description",
        ),
    )

However, a migration is required only if it is a breaking change for your users.

docs.title: Warning: dependency changes
docs.text:
Note that changing FastAPI endpoint dependencies is only going to affect the initial validation. Cadwyn will run your altered dependencies for each request to the endpoint but ultimately your endpoint code is always going to use the HEAD version of your dependencies. So be careful.

Also note that if some of your dependencies are added at app/router level, they are going to be overwritten by the instructions above. Most of the time it is rather safe, however, as all the necessary dependencies will still run on HEAD version.

docs.title: WebSocket endpoint migrations
docs.text:
Use ["WEBSOCKET"] to select a FastAPI WebSocket route defined with @router.websocket(). It supports .didnt_exist, .existed, and .had(path=..., name=..., dependencies=...). Mark sockets that only exist in older versions with @router.only_exists_in_older_versions, just like HTTP endpoints.

from cadwyn import (
    Cadwyn,
    Version,
    VersionBundle,
    VersionChange,
    VersionedAPIRouter,
    endpoint,
)
from fastapi import Depends, Header, WebSocket


async def current_token(token: str = Header()):
    return token


async def legacy_token(legacy_token: str = Header()):
    return legacy_token


router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.websocket(
    "/ws/{room}", name="room", dependencies=[Depends(current_token)]
)
async def room_socket(websocket: WebSocket, room: str):
    await websocket.accept()
    await websocket.send_json({"room": room})
    await websocket.close()


@router.websocket("/notifications")
async def notifications(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()
    await websocket.send_text("notification")
    await websocket.close()


@router.only_exists_in_older_versions
@router.websocket("/legacy")
async def legacy_socket(websocket: WebSocket):
    await websocket.accept()
    await websocket.send_text("legacy")
    await websocket.close()


class UpdateSockets(VersionChange):
    description = "Move chat connections and their token header; replace the legacy socket."
    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        endpoint("/ws/{room}", ["WEBSOCKET"]).had(
            path="/chat/{room}",
            name="chat",
            dependencies=[Depends(legacy_token)],
        ),
        endpoint("/notifications", ["WEBSOCKET"]).didnt_exist,
        endpoint("/legacy", ["WEBSOCKET"]).existed,
    )


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(
        Version("2024-02-01", UpdateSockets), Version("2024-01-01")
    )
)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

In this example, clients of 2024-02-01 connect to /ws/general with the token header. Clients of 2024-01-01 connect to /chat/general with legacy-token instead. The older version also keeps /legacy and has no /notifications socket. Both clients pass their API version in the x-api-version header; path versioning and constant defaults also work.

Unlike HTTP endpoints, WebSockets run only the dependencies of the selected version, including dependency overrides and cleanup. .had(dependencies=...) replaces the route's dependency list, including dependencies inherited from included routers. Dependencies declared in the endpoint signature still run. A path change must keep the same path parameter names. Use func_name to distinguish sockets with the same path, as in the endpoint duplicates example below.

WEBSOCKET must be the only method in its selector, and .had() accepts only path, name, and dependencies for sockets. Other attributes and mixed HTTP/WebSocket selectors raise an error when the instruction is defined. Request and response data converters remain HTTP-only.

WebSockets stay out of OpenAPI. Cadwyn does not apply schema or message migrations to WebSocket connections; handle message formats in your endpoint code. These instructions support FastAPI APIWebSocketRoute routes only: plain Starlette WebSocketRoutes (@router.websocket_route()), plain Starlette Routes, Mount, and static files are outside their scope.

docs.title: Dealing with endpoint duplicates
docs.text:
Sometimes, when making advanced changes between versions, you need to rewrite your endpoint function entirely. So essentially you would have the following structure:

from typing import Annotated

from cadwyn import VersionedAPIRouter
from fastapi import Header
from fastapi.params import Param

router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.only_exists_in_older_versions
@router.get("/users")
def get_users_by_name_before_starting_to_use_params(
    user_name: Annotated[str, Header()],
):
    """Some code that references user_name"""


@router.get("/users")
def get_users_by_name(user_name: Annotated[str, Param()]):
    """Some code that references user_name"""

As you can see in the code example above, the two functions have the same parameters and path decorators. And if you have many versions, you may have even more functions like these two. The recommended way to instruct Cadwyn to restore one of them and delete the other is the following:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, endpoint


class UseParamsInsteadOfHeadersForUserNameFiltering(VersionChange):
    """'GET /users' now accepts the user-name filter as a query parameter
    instead of a header, following standard HTTP filtering conventions.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        # Specify the name; otherwise you will encounter an exception due to
        # having two identical endpoints with the same parameters and path decorators
        endpoint(
            "/users",
            ["GET"],
            func_name="get_users_by_name_before_starting_to_use_params",
        ).existed,
        # Also specify the name here because, following the instructions above,
        # we now have two existing endpoints
        endpoint("/users", ["GET"], func_name="get_users_by_name").didnt_exist,
    )
Using a more specific func_name allows to distinguish between different functions that affect the same routes.

docs.title: Enum migrations
docs.text: The instructions below affect only OpenAPI schemas and their initial validation. All of your incoming requests will still be converted to your HEAD schemas.

docs.title: Adding enum members
docs.text:
Note that adding enum members can be a breaking change in contrast to adding optional fields to a schema. For example, if you return a list of entities, each of which has some type, and you add a new type, then your clients' code is likely to break.

It is recommended to add enum members in new versions as well.

from enum import Enum

from cadwyn import VersionChange, enum


class MyEnum(str, Enum):
    baz = "baz"
    foo = "foo"
    bar = "bar"


class AddFooAndBarToMyEnum(VersionChange):
    """'MyEnum' now includes 'foo' and 'bar' so clients can represent the
    newly supported states.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        enum(MyEnum).didnt_have("foo", "bar"),
    )

docs.title: Removing enum members
docs.text:
from enum import Enum

from cadwyn import VersionChange, enum


class MyEnum(str, Enum):
    qux = "qux"


class RemoveFooAndBarFromMyEnum(VersionChange):
    """'foo' and 'bar' are no longer returned in 'MyEnum' because those
    legacy states are no longer supported.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        enum(MyEnum).had(foo="baz", bar="bar"),
    )

docs.title: How Cadwyn copies enums
docs.text:
For every version, Cadwyn copies the enums that have enum(...) instructions. A copy behaves like the enum that you would write by hand for that version: it keeps aliases, nonmember() attributes, and @member functions, and had() takes the same values that you would write in the class body.

Copies retain constructor-produced state for their version, even when construction deliberately leaves an attribute unset. Unchanged members keep extra attributes and slots assigned outside construction, such as labels added after class creation or by a metaclass. Replaced members and aliases that become canonical members are constructed for their version instead of inheriting the old member's state. Cadwyn runs your enum's __new__ and __init__ again while it copies the enum, possibly several times per version, so don't rely on side effects of construction such as a global counter.

Known limitation: enum-valued members are unwrapped in generated copies, including values passed to had(). For example, if Outer.a = Inner.a, the copy stores Inner.a.value rather than Inner.a; members whose raw values compare equal can become aliases. This behavior is retained to preserve existing requests, responses, validation errors, and OpenAPI. Use raw values directly when defining versioned enums.

Cadwyn does not replay a metaclass declared only on the enum itself: metaclasses can require class-creation arguments that the enum has not stored. Members added with had() and aliases that become canonical members can therefore lack attributes assigned only by the metaclass. Use a property or member constructor for attributes that these members need.

had(member=auto()) uses the enum's _generate_next_value_; use explicit values to preserve values from an earlier Cadwyn release. Plain enums and flags accept latest-version members with matching values (including flag combinations with no unknown bits), before trying _missing_. Request migrations still see the client version's members; endpoints get the latest members, so compare union fields to members rather than raw values.

Cadwyn only knows the values of the members, not the arguments that they were defined with. So an enum with a custom __new__ that sets attributes from more than the value (e.g. mass from earth = (1, 5.97) for __new__(cls, value, mass)) can't be copied, and Cadwyn raises a SchemaGenerationError at startup. Overwriting attributes that its constructor sets also fails this check. Compute such attributes from the value instead, e.g. with a property:

from enum import Enum

from cadwyn import VersionChange, enum

_LABELS = {"red": "Red", "green": "Green", "blue": "Blue"}


class Color(str, Enum):
    red = "red"
    green = "green"
    blue = "blue"

    @property
    def label(self) -> str:
        return _LABELS[self.value]


class RemoveBlueFromColor(VersionChange):
    """'blue' is a new color."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        enum(Color).didnt_have("blue"),
    )

Plain enums and flags with enum(...) instructions can be used in supported lazy request fields such as Iterable[Kind] and Generator[Kind, None, None]. Cadwyn converts their members to the latest enum as the endpoint consumes them; unconsumed items stay unvalidated. Request migrations still see the request version's members. Conversion leaves unions with alternative branches and opaque validation paths unchanged; see known limitations.

Strict response validation still rejects latest enum members when enum(...) instructions create a distinct enum class for the response version, including optional fields and nested models or containers. Use Field(strict=False) on affected response fields or a response migration that supplies the client's own members. Cadwyn retains the previous enum schemas: custom schema hooks, unions with alternative branches, value-based enums (str, int, or float), and OpenAPI keep their existing behavior. Adding a normalization wrapper for strict responses can change the schemas observed by hooks, including cached nested models, so strict responses remain a known limitation.

docs.title: Main App
docs.text:
Cadwyn's standard usage involves a single customized FastAPI app: cadwyn.Cadwyn. It accepts the same arguments as fastapi.FastAPI plus several additional keyword-only arguments. The most important ones are:

  • Required versions: VersionBundle describes all versions of your app
  • Optional api_version_parameter_name: str = "x-api-version" is the parameter that Cadwyn uses for routing to different API versions of your app

After you have defined the main app, you can add versioned API routers to it using Cadwyn.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(*routers)

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle, VersionedAPIRouter

my_version_bundle = VersionBundle(Version("2022-11-16"))
router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.get("/users/", tags=["users"])
async def read_users():
    return [{"username": "Rick"}, {"username": "Morty"}]


@router.get("/users/{username}", tags=["users"])
async def read_user(username: str):
    return {"username": username}


app = Cadwyn(versions=my_version_bundle)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

That's it. generate_and_include_versioned_routers() will generate all versions of your routers based on the versions argument.

docs.title: Routing
docs.text:
Cadwyn is built on header-based routing. First, requests are routed to the appropriate API version based on the version header (x-api-version by default). Second, requests are routed by the appropriate url path and method. By default, Cadwyn uses ISO 8601 date-based versions (such as 2022-11-16), but it also supports arbitrary strings as versions. If a user provides a date that does not match any of the versions exactly, Cadwyn selects the closest earlier applicable version. For example, 2022-11-16 in a request can be matched by 2022-11-15 or 2000-01-01 but not by 2022-11-17.

However, header-based routing is the default way to use Cadwyn. Cadwyn can also take the version from a URL path parameter. If you want to use any other form of routing, you can use Cadwyn directly through cadwyn.generate_versioned_routers() or subclass cadwyn.Cadwyn with a different router and middleware. Remember to update the VersionBundle.api_version_var variable each time you route a request to a version. This variable allows Cadwyn to do side effects and data migrations.

docs.title: VersionedAPIRouter
docs.text: Cadwyn has its own API Router class: cadwyn.VersionedAPIRouter. You are free to use a regular fastapi.APIRouter but cadwyn.VersionedAPIRouter has a special decorator only_exists_in_older_versions(route) which allows you to define routes that have been previously deleted. First you define the route and then add this decorator to it.

docs.title: Using fastapi-pagination
docs.text:
add_pagination(app) from fastapi-pagination does not work with Cadwyn's versioned routes: either the app fails to start with AttributeError: __params_type__, or paginated endpoints fail with UninitializedConfigurationError. Instead, call add_pagination() on your VersionedAPIRouter before you include it:

from fastapi_pagination import Page, add_pagination, paginate

router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.get("/users")
async def list_users() -> Page[User]:
    return paginate(get_users())


add_pagination(router)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

Alternatively, pass the pagination params to paginate() explicitly:

from typing import Annotated

from fastapi import Depends
from fastapi_pagination import Page, Params, paginate


@router.get("/users")
async def list_users(params: Annotated[Params, Depends()]) -> Page[User]:
    return paginate(get_users(), params)

docs.title: Customizing OpenAPI
docs.text:
Pass a synchronous openapi_customizer callback to Cadwyn() to edit each version's OpenAPI document. It receives the generated schema and the selected version as a string, or None for /openapi.json?version=unversioned. Cadwyn calls it after its own adjustments, including required version headers and servers for mounted apps or a proxy's root path, immediately before serialization.

For example, add a component used by a client SDK even though no endpoint references it, only in the version that needs it:

from typing import Any, Union

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle, VersionedAPIRouter
from pydantic import BaseModel


class TaskMetadata(BaseModel):
    trace_id: str


def customize_openapi(
    schema: dict[str, Any], version: Union[str, None]
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    if version == "2024-01-01":
        schemas = schema.setdefault("components", {}).setdefault("schemas", {})
        schemas["TaskMetadata"] = TaskMetadata.model_json_schema()
    return schema


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2024-01-01"), Version("2023-01-01")),
    openapi_customizer=customize_openapi,
)
router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.get("/tasks")
def get_tasks() -> list[str]:
    return ["example-task"]


app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

Return the edited dict or a replacement dict. Any other return value, including None, raises a TypeError naming the callback; exceptions raised by the callback propagate. Each request gets a freshly generated dict, and Cadwyn does not cache customized schemas. Omitting the callback or passing None preserves the existing output. The callback type is available as cadwyn.OpenAPICustomizer.

docs.title: Custom docs static assets
docs.text:
By default, Swagger UI and ReDoc load JavaScript and CSS from CDNs. You can override these URLs to serve assets locally:

app = Cadwyn(
    versions=my_version_bundle,
    swagger_js_url="/static/swagger-ui-bundle.js",
    swagger_css_url="/static/swagger-ui.css",
    swagger_favicon_url="/static/favicon.png",
    redoc_js_url="/static/redoc.standalone.js",
    redoc_favicon_url="/static/favicon.png",
)

docs.title: Methodology
docs.text:
Cadwyn implements a methodology that is based on the following set of principles:

  • Each version consists of "version changes" or "compatibility gates" which describe independent, atomic differences from the previous version
  • A new version is created if and only if there are breaking changes
  • Versions must have little to no effect on the business logic
  • Versions must always be compatible in terms of data
  • Creating new versions is avoided at all costs
  • Any backward-compatible features must be backported to all compatible versions

Following these rules enables you to have a large number of self-documenting versions while encapsulating their complexity in small version change classes, providing your users with a consistent and stable experience.

If a breaking change cannot be avoided, the general approach is to:

  1. Introduce the breaking change in your schemas, routes, or business logic
  2. Write a version change class (and sometimes a little extra) that describes the difference between the new version and the old version

docs.title: Schema generation
docs.text: Cadwyn automatically generates versioned schemas and everything related to them from HEAD version at runtime — no code is actually generated. These versioned schemas will be automatically used in requests to and responses from versioned API routes.

docs.title: Rendering schemas
docs.text:
If you have many versions and schemas, it is quite challenging to know what validators, fields, and other attributes are defined in each schema in a specific version. To address this issue, there is a way to render the generated Pydantic models and enums as code using the command-line interface.

NOTICE that cadwyn render does not guarantee rendering correct schemas. It provides a close enough approximation for manual validation, but it is not yet ready for production code generation. For example, it doesn't handle schema renaming in a class's __bases__ yet.

docs.title: Rendering a module
docs.text:
Here's a way to render the entire module with the schemas:

cadwyn render module data.schemas --app=main:app --version=2024-05-26

This command prints to stdout how the schemas would look in version 2024-05-26 if they were written by hand rather than generated at runtime by Cadwyn. This command takes the schemas from data/schemas.py module and knows what the schemas would look based on the version changes from Cadwyn app instance named app and located in main.py. Run it from the directory that contains main.py and data/: cadwyn imports the modules from there.

docs.title: Rendering a single model
docs.text:
Here's a way to render a single Pydantic model or enum with the schemas:

cadwyn render model data.schemas:UserCreateRequest --app=main:app --version=2024-05-26

This command prints to stdout how the UserCreateRequest schema would look in version 2024-05-26 if it was written by hand rather than generated at runtime by Cadwyn. This command takes the UserCreateRequest schema from data/schemas.py module and knows what the schema would look based on the version changes from Cadwyn app instance named app and located in main.py.

The rendered fields are the ones that the schema has in that version. When a schema has instructions for a field that it inherits, it is rendered with its own version of that field, and its parents and siblings are rendered with theirs (see Fields that a schema inherits).

Rendering supports named tuples defined with NamedTuple or collections.namedtuple, defaultdict (with a type, a named Python function, or None as its factory), and Counter defaults. Nested builtin containers retain references such as None and types instead of quoting them as strings. As with other references in rendered models, make the referenced classes and functions available when executing the output.

Changed model configs render named functions by reference and inline lambdas supplied through their config key, such as ConfigDict(json_schema_extra=lambda s: s.update({"x-legacy": True})). Config callables require plain immutable scalar defaults; lambda defaults must also appear as matching literals in their source. Their function references, free variables, and global bindings must resolve to the same objects in the rendered module. Unavailable or ambiguous lambda source, nonliteral defaults, and captured state or bindings that cannot be verified raise CadwynRenderError naming the model and config key. Use a module-level named function with literal defaults and resolvable globals instead. These checks apply only to config callables; rendering of default_factory callables is unchanged.

Recursive containers and shared builtin or standard-library mutable containers raise CadwynRenderError, as do OrderedDict and Counter defaults with extra instance attributes, unsupported defaultdict factories (such as lambdas or callable instances), and subclasses whose representations lose their type by printing a builtin container literal. Use Field(default_factory=...) with a named function that creates the whole value for these defaults.

Container subclass expressions and the new named-tuple, defaultdict, and Counter paths are checked by reconstructing their source with the model's referenced types and comparing contents, types, and instance state. Rendering raises CadwynRenderError if it cannot verify fidelity; use a named factory for such values. Repeated immutable containers and the formatting of correctly rendered defaults are preserved. Nonfinite floats use executable float('inf'), float('-inf'), and float('nan') expressions.

docs.title: Generating schemas without FastAPI
docs.text:
Cadwyn can generate versioned schemas from its version changes even without FastAPI:

from cadwyn import Version, VersionBundle, VersionChange, schema
from cadwyn.schema_generation import generate_versioned_models
from pydantic import BaseModel


class MyVersionedSchema(BaseModel):
    full_name: str


class RenameNameToFullName(VersionChange):
    description = "Renamed `name` to `full_name`"
    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MyVersionedSchema).field("full_name").had(name="name"),
    )


version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    Version("2026-01-01", RenameNameToFullName),
    Version("2025-11-16"),
)

schema_generators = generate_versioned_models(version_bundle)
MyVersionedSchemaFrom2025 = schema_generators["2025-11-16"][MyVersionedSchema]

Cadwyn generates a copy of every model for every version, except for the enums without enum instructions and the models that refer to themselves (directly or through other models, e.g. children: "list[Category]") when neither they nor the models they refer to have instructions in any version (including HeadVersion) and they are not parents of models with versioned copies. Cadwyn uses such enums and models as they are: schema_generators["2025-11-16"][Category] is Category. Cadwyn makes this decision when it first needs a model, so the models defined after that (e.g. new subclasses) do not change it.

docs.title: Bases supplied through __mro_entries__
docs.text:
Models whose bases are supplied by an object's __mro_entries__ hook use the versioned parents when the resolved bases match the original model's bases and those parents are complete models affected by schema instructions for that version. The parents' schema instructions and the checks for inherited fields then apply as they do to explicit base classes. When upgrading from Cadwyn 8, update affected request and response migrations to use the corrected older-version fields.

Cadwyn calls these hooks again while it copies models, possibly several times per version, so a hook must return the same bases every time and must not rely on how often it is called. Dynamically resolved, incomplete, or unmatched bases keep their previous behavior; use explicit base classes if you need schema instructions to reach those parents reliably.

docs.title: Generic models
docs.text:
Parametrized generic models such as Page[Item] use the versioned copies of their type args in every version. For example, take the app from issue #416:

from typing import Generic, TypeVar

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, Version, VersionBundle, VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Item(BaseModel):
    full_name: str


T = TypeVar("T", bound=Item)


class Page(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
    items: list[T]


class RenameNameToFullName(VersionChange):
    description = "Renamed `name` to `full_name`"
    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(Item).field("full_name").had(name="name"),
    )


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(
        Version("2001-01-01", RenameNameToFullName),
        Version("2000-01-01"),
    )
)

Version 2000-01-01 uses the old Item with its name field inside Page[Item], generic subclasses such as PageWithTotal[Item], class ItemPage(Page[Item]), class Items(RootModel[list[Item]]), and nested generics such as Page[Page[Item]], and its OpenAPI has one Item schema.

Only the generics whose type args refer to models or enums that have schema or enum instructions in any version, including HeadVersion, are affected. All other generics keep their type args, their OpenAPI names, and their behavior. Cadwyn 7 kept the latest versions of the type args in every version, so apps that have such generics change when they upgrade:

  • Older versions validate and serialize the args with their old models, so clients of older versions that relied on the latest models inside generics may get validation errors. Converters for Item do not run for the items of Page[Item], so add converters for the generics too where older clients need them, e.g. convert_response_to_previous_version_for(Page[Item]) and convert_request_to_next_version_for(Page[Item]) that rename full_name to name and back in every item.
  • Changes from HeadVersion also apply to these args in every version, including the latest one.
  • The OpenAPI names of these generics can change in every version because their quoted type args are evaluated, e.g. Page[list["Item"]] is named Page_list_Item__ instead of Page_list_str__.
  • migrate_response_body rejects instances of the latest models inside these generics, e.g. Page[Item](...) or {"items": [Item(...)]} for Page[Item], with a ValidationError in every version, including the latest one, as it already does for other versioned models nested in the response model. Pass plain data, such as the result of model_dump(), instead.
  • The models in these args are copied for every version like other versioned models, so the ones that cannot be copied (e.g. with an Annotated validator that holds a threading.Lock, which cannot be deep-copied) fail even if no route uses them directly.
  • Instructions for a specific parametrization, such as schema(Pair[str, int]), also apply where pydantic builds that parametrization in a field of another generic, such as pair: Pair[T, int] in Box[T] used as Box[str] (issue #420). Cadwyn 7 kept Pair[str, int] without its instructions there in older versions of Box[str]. Now request bodies with Box[str] need the same request migrations as Pair[str, int] itself. Fields keep their previous behavior when Box, its bases, or Box[str] have instructions of their own, when pydantic refers to the parametrization recursively inside itself, or when such parametrizations refer to each other.
  • Instructions for a field that a model inherits from a generic base through its type args keep the field's type in older versions. For example, schema(Ints).field("root").had(description=...) for class Ints(RootModel[list[int]]), or schema(StrIntPair).field("second").had(...) for class StrIntPair(Pair[str, int]). In Cadwyn 7, such a field became the bare type var (~RootModelRootType, ~U) in older versions, so they accepted any value for it, and invalid input failed with a 500 instead of a 422. Now the field behaves in older versions like any other field of its type, so requests that only worked because it accepted anything can change:
    • its validators and coercion run in the older version as well as in the latest one, as for other fields, so validators that are not idempotent, e.g. AfterValidator(lambda v: v + 1) in the type args, apply more than once;
    • serializers that change its value, e.g. PlainSerializer(lambda v: f"{v:,}", return_type=str), also change the request body that reaches the latest version, so such requests need request migrations;
    • models in its type args validate their older shape, e.g. after schema(Item).field("n").had(name="old_n") the older version requires old_n;
    • request migrations run after the older version validates the field, so they no longer see values that its type rejects.
    • as for other fields, had() does not change the constraints that the field's type declares through Annotated[..., Field(...)], e.g. in its type arg or in the annotation of the parent that defines it. So on Pydantic 2.12 and newer, .had(ge=5) for a field whose type carries Annotated[int, Field(ge=0)] no longer applies, and older versions accept values such as 1 that they rejected before.

Generic models used without type args, such as Page in the example above, use the versioned models and enums in the bounds, constraints, or defaults of parameters that their fields actually validate. The same applies to unresolved parameters in partially specialized generics and unparametrized type aliases. Fully parametrized models such as Page[Item] and Payload[int] keep their existing type-argument versioning and never version the bounds of the parameters that those arguments replace. Unused parameters keep their original behavior.

Older versions now reject the latest shape when it differs from their own (issue #584). Add request and response converters for the outer generic, or for the endpoint's path, wherever the nested data needs migrating; converters for the nested model do not run automatically. Affected bare generics can have different OpenAPI names, such as Page[T].

Quoted bounds resolve in each consuming model's namespace or the type alias's module. Cadwyn keeps generic templates and their original parameters intact, including for self-referencing generics. Parameters whose fallback refers back to their consuming model retain the existing recursive-model versioning behavior. A bare generic whose validation fallback cannot be resolved or safely versioned raises SchemaGenerationError; use explicit type arguments for such a model.

TypeVar-based typed extra fields (__pydantic_extra__ with extra="allow") remain a known limitation: older versions can still validate and document their latest bounds. Use a concrete annotation such as __pydantic_extra__: dict[str, Item] on a non-generic model instead.

Some type args keep their latest models:

  • the args that lead back to the generic itself, e.g. subcategories: Page["Category"] within Category (see Models that refer to each other);
  • the args whose models refer to names that are not defined yet when Cadwyn first needs the generic;
  • quoted args, such as Page["Item"], whose models are not defined in the module of the generic.

docs.title: Computed fields that return models
docs.text:
Pydantic resolves the return types of computed fields on its own, so Cadwyn cannot version them: in every version, a computed field that returns a versioned model (a model with instructions, or one that refers to such models) keeps the latest version of that model. In older versions, this has two consequences:

  • The computed field serializes the data that it returns with the latest model. If it returns the versioned data of the model, e.g. self.items[0] in def best(self) -> Item, the fields that the older version renamed or changed are left out or appear in their latest shape.
  • OpenAPI describes the computed field with the latest model too.

If older versions need the older shape of such data, expose it as a regular field instead of a computed field, e.g. best: Item filled in by a validator or by the endpoint. Cadwyn versions regular fields and migrates their data like any other.

docs.title: Defaults
docs.text:
Every version gets its own copies of the lists, tuples, and dicts in the defaults of fields and of the params of endpoints and dependencies. Plain lists, tuples, and dicts get rebuilt, so where they hold a model class, an enum class, or a function, e.g. default=[Item], the copy holds the version's own Item. Any other subclass of list, tuple, or dict (e.g. a NamedTuple, an OrderedDict, a defaultdict, or your own class), and any list, tuple, or dict that contains itself, gets its own copy.deepcopy() in every version, with its type and attributes, as Pydantic copies mutable defaults. Cadwyn can't rebuild such a container with the version's copies, so it raises a SchemaGenerationError if the container holds a model class (every version has its own copies of all models), an enum class with instructions, a function or another callable (except the ones from FastAPI, Pydantic, and Starlette, and the ones without an inspectable signature), or a type that contains one of them (e.g. list[Item] or Annotated[int, Item]), or if deepcopy fails. The same applies to the other attributes of fields, such as examples and json_schema_extra, and to the metadata of Annotated. Cadwyn doesn't look into any other objects in defaults, so they keep the latest classes (see Known limitations).

A default factory whose defaults contain a container leading back to that factory cannot be copied and raises SchemaGenerationError; break that reference cycle.

docs.title: Models that refer to each other
docs.text:
Models can refer to themselves, directly or through other models, e.g. children: "list[Category]" or Author.books: list[Book] with Book.author: Author. When such models need versioning, Cadwyn copies all of them together, and their copies refer to each other. So if Category had a title field instead of name in an older version, that version uses title at every depth of the tree.

Parametrized generic models such as Page[Category] use these copies as their type args when the models with instructions or the routes of the version refer to such models. Otherwise, e.g. when such models only need versioning because they refer to a model with instructions and only migrate_response_body uses them directly, the type args of generics keep the latest models, as they always did. If a model with instructions refers to such models only through the type args of a generic, while a route uses them directly, Cadwyn raises a SchemaGenerationError instead of using both the latest and the older versions of them in one version.

Cadwyn raises a SchemaGenerationError when it generates the versions if it cannot copy such models:

  • when they refer to each other in places that need the classes themselves rather than annotations, e.g. in default factories, in the metadata of Annotated, in type aliases, or in the type args of generics that are not from typing or collections.abc;
  • when their copies, or the other copies of the version that use them, would still use the latest versions of such models, which Cadwyn cannot version there: e.g. in the return types of computed fields and serializers, in names quoted inside other annotations (list["Book"], which you can write as "list[Book]" instead), in generic fields whose type args lead back to the generic itself, such as children: Page["Category"] in a Category that also refers to itself in another way, or in a generic that keeps the latest models next to a field that uses their copies, such as category: Category along with related: Page[Category] when only migrate_response_body uses them;
  • when a field of such a model that uses models that need versioning, or a field of another model that uses such models, has a default that contains an instance of the latest version of a model that needs versioning (e.g. settings: Settings = Settings(), also within other models and containers), or a default factory that Cadwyn cannot verify. Cadwyn only accepts list, dict, set, tuple, and frozenset, the classes of the models themselves (e.g. Field(default_factory=Settings), which Cadwyn versions), pydantic's constructors of the models that do not need versioning (e.g. Unchanged.model_construct), and functools.partial of these with arguments that pass the same check. The defaults of all other fields are used as Cadwyn always did, except that their values must not contain the latest versions of such models (e.g. raw: dict = {"category": Category(...)}). Enum members are serialized by their values so they are used as Cadwyn always did;
  • when their annotations, or the annotations of the functions that they use, refer to names that are not defined yet.

Some other things to keep in mind about such models:

  • Cadwyn cannot see the latest models that validators create, e.g. AfterValidator(lambda value: Settings()). As with all other models, their older versions keep such latest models.
  • Their copies are built when Cadwyn generates them, even if they use defer_build=True.
  • Their hooks that Pydantic calls while it builds them, such as __pydantic_init_subclass__, must not ask Cadwyn for their own versioned copies (e.g. through migrate_response_body): Cadwyn raises a CadwynError if they do.
  • The schema hooks of any model (e.g. __get_pydantic_core_schema__) must not ask Cadwyn for versioned models while another thread generates the versioned copies of such models: Pydantic 2.14 holds its lock while it runs these hooks, and Cadwyn rebuilds such copies while it holds its own lock.

docs.title: Schema migrations
docs.text:
The following instructions affect only OpenAPI schemas and their initial validation. All your incoming requests will still be converted to your HEAD schemas.

Please note that you only need a migration if it is a breaking change for your users. The scenarios below only describe "what you can do" but not "what you should do". For the "should" part, please refer to the how-to docs.

docs.title: SQLAlchemy and SQLModel classes
docs.text:
Cadwyn leaves SQLAlchemy and SQLModel classes unchanged when generating API versions. This includes SQLModel classes with or without table=True. You can use these classes in dependencies, request bodies, and response models where FastAPI supports them, but their schemas remain the same across API versions.

schema(...) and the schema-based forms of convert_request_to_next_version_for(...) and convert_response_to_previous_version_for(...) reject these classes with a CadwynStructureError. To version their API representation, define a separate Pydantic BaseModel.

docs.title: Add a field to the older version
docs.text:
from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import Field


class RemoveFooFromMySchema(VersionChange):
    """'MySchema.foo' has been removed because clients no longer need the
    legacy list of values.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema)
        .field("foo")
        .existed_as(type=list[str], info=Field(description="Foo")),
    )

docs.title: Remove a field from the older version
docs.text:
from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema


class AddFooToMySchema(VersionChange):
    """'MySchema.foo' is now available so clients can read the value directly
    instead of deriving it from other fields.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema).field("foo").didnt_exist,
    )

A pydantic model can't drop a field that it inherits. So if a subclass declares a field again or changed it in a newer version, schema(Subclass).field(...).didnt_exist for it fails at startup with an InvalidGenerationInstructionError that names the parent if the parent still has the field in that version. Delete the field from the parent in the same version instead, which deletes it from all of its subclasses.

docs.title: Change a field in the older version
docs.text:
The following code sets an attribute of a field, such as a description:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema


class ChangeMySchemaFooDescription(VersionChange):
    """The documentation for 'MySchema.foo' now explains the field's purpose
    so clients can interpret its value correctly.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema).field("foo").had(description="Foo"),
    )

The following code un-sets an attribute of a field, as if it never existed:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema


class AddDescriptionToMySchemaFoo(VersionChange):
    """'MySchema.foo' now has a documented meaning so clients do not need to
    infer how to use it.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema).field("foo").didnt_have("description"),
    )

Instructions reject unchanged values, but distinguish values such as True and 1, -0.0 and 0.0, or Decimal("1.0") and Decimal("1.00"). They compare supported builtin values, containers, and type hints without calling user comparison methods; sequence and dict order matters, and unknown objects use identity. Passing the very same object is always redundant, even for NaN.

ALIAS WARNING:

Pydantic copies a field's alias into its validation_alias and serialization_alias unless you pass them. Like Field(), .had(alias=...) and .didnt_have("alias") change these copies too, so the older version uses the new key in requests, responses, and OpenAPI. Aliases equal to the original alias follow it too, even if passed explicitly in Field(). Other explicit aliases stay as they are; an instruction can also set them explicitly to keep the newer key, e.g. .had(alias="legacy", validation_alias="a", serialization_alias="a") for Field(alias="a"). .didnt_have() keeps the aliases of a Field() in Annotated, e.g. Annotated[str, Field(alias="foo_key")], like its other attributes that don't only document the field, unless the module uses from __future__ import annotations. So an alias change needs request and response migrations that rename the key:

from cadwyn import (
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class MySchema(BaseModel):
    foo: str = Field(alias="foo_key")


class RenameFooKey(VersionChange):
    description = (
        "Renamed the key of 'MySchema.foo' from 'old_foo_key' to 'foo_key'"
    )
    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema).field("foo").had(alias="old_foo_key"),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(MySchema)
    def rename_old_foo_key(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["foo_key"] = request.body.pop("old_foo_key")

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(MySchema)
    def rename_foo_key(response: ResponseInfo):
        response.body["old_foo_key"] = response.body.pop("foo_key")

If the data that the older version validates has the key that the field had before the instruction but not its new key, e.g. because a client still sends the old key or a migration is missing, Cadwyn fails instead of giving the field its default: requests get a 422, and responses fail with a ResponseValidationError (a 500). Cadwyn decides this from the data as it comes in, so this also happens when a validator of the model fills the field from other keys. To keep the old key in the older version instead, remove the alias change from the instruction.

DEFAULTS WARNING:

If you add default or default_factory to the old version of a schema, it will not manifest in the code automatically. Instead, you should add the default or default_factory, and then also add the default value using a request migration.

The reason for such behaviour is the way Cadwyn works with Pydantic and unfortunately this cannot be changed:

Cadwyn:

  1. Receives a request for API version V
  2. Validates the request using the schemas from V
  3. Marshalls the unmarshalled request body into a raw data structure using BaseModel.model_dump with exclude_unset=True and without computed fields, which latest computes itself
  4. Passes the request through all request migrations from V to latest
  5. Validates the request using latest schemas

The part that causes the aforementioned problem is Cadwyn's use of exclude_unset=True. Unfortunately, when Cadwyn uses it, default fields are not set, so latest does not receive them. And if latest does not have the same defaults (for example, if the field has no default and is required in latest), then an error will occur. If Cadwyn used exclude_unset=False, then exclude_unset would lose its purpose for Cadwyn users, so giving it up is impractical. Instead, you should set all extras in step 4 in your request migrations.

docs.title: Fields that a schema inherits
docs.text:
.had(...) and .didnt_have(...) for a field that a schema inherits change the field only in that schema and its subclasses, not in its parents or its siblings:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Invoice(BaseModel):
    code: str


class BusinessInvoice(Invoice):
    pass


class PersonalInvoice(Invoice):
    pass


class AllowLongBusinessInvoiceCodes(VersionChange):
    """Business invoice codes can now be longer than 5 characters."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BusinessInvoice).field("code").had(max_length=5),
    )

In the older version, BusinessInvoice.code has max_length=5, while Invoice.code and PersonalInvoice.code stay unchanged. To change the field in all of these schemas, give the instruction to the parent: schema(Invoice).field("code").had(max_length=5). Renames don't work this way. A pydantic model can't drop a field that it inherits, so had(name=...) in a subclass for a field that its parent still has, in that version or in an older one, fails at startup with an InvalidGenerationInstructionError that names the parent. Rename the field in the schema that declares it instead: schema(Invoice).field("code").had(name="number") renames it in Invoice, BusinessInvoice, and PersonalInvoice. If a subclass changed the field in a newer version (e.g. schema(BusinessInvoice).field("code").had(max_length=5)) or declares it again (e.g. code: str in BusinessInvoice), rename it in that subclass and in the parent in the same version. The subclass then keeps its own changes under the new name. Otherwise, it would keep the old field next to the renamed one, so Cadwyn fails at startup with an InvalidGenerationInstructionError that names the subclass. The same happens when a subclass gets a field with the old name from another base, e.g. a mixin.

To preserve both names instead of renaming an inherited field, use schema(Child).field("y").existed_as(type=..., info=Field(...)) with the attributes of Child.x. If Child redeclares x, also restore its type and attributes to the parent's values with .had(...) and remove child-only attributes with .didnt_have(...), including constraints in Annotated. Deleting a field with .didnt_exist likewise fails if the schema would still inherit it: delete it from the base in the same version too.

The changes of a parent's field also apply to its subclasses, including the ones that changed the field themselves, with these exceptions:

  • A subclass that already has an instruction of its own for the field, in a newer version or earlier in the same version change, keeps the type and the Annotated metadata that the field had at that point. So a later had(type=...) of a parent, listed after it or in an older version, doesn't change the type of the field in that subclass.
  • If the schema that declares the field has no instructions of its own and no request migrations (convert_request_to_next_version_for(...)), the changes that a schema between it and the subclass makes, listed after the subclass's change or in an older version, don't reach a subclass that changed the field itself. Any instruction for the declaring schema, e.g. for another field, makes them apply.

The same holds for generic schemas: an instruction for a parametrization such as schema(Page[Item]) changes Page[Item] and its subclasses, but not Page or its other parametrizations.

In multiple inheritance, such as class D(C, B), D takes each field from its first base that has it, as in pydantic. So for a field that both C and B have, e.g. from their common parent, the instructions given only for B don't apply to D unless D changes that field itself. Give the instruction to the common parent, or to D as well. The instructions for a field that only B has, e.g. because B declares it, apply to D as usual.

docs.title: Add a validator to the older version
docs.text:
from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import field_validator


@field_validator("foo")
def validate_foo(cls, value):
    if ":" not in value:
        raise ValueError("foo must contain a colon")
    return value


class RemoveFooValidatorFromMySchema(VersionChange):
    """'MySchema.foo' no longer requires colon-separated values because the
    field now accepts plain text.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema).validator(validate_foo).existed,
    )

docs.title: Remove a validator from the older version
docs.text:
from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema


class AddFooValidatorToMySchema(VersionChange):
    """'MySchema.foo' must now contain a colon to distinguish the value's two
    components.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema).validator(MySchema.validate_foo).didnt_exist,
    )

To remove a validator assigned as a class attribute, pass the attribute name:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator


def must_be_positive(value: int) -> int:
    if value <= 0:
        raise ValueError("must be positive")
    return value


class Dimensions(BaseModel):
    width: int
    height: int

    check_width = field_validator("width")(must_be_positive)
    check_height = field_validator("height")(must_be_positive)


class RequirePositiveWidth(VersionChange):
    """Width must now be positive, as height already was."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(Dimensions).validator("check_width").didnt_exist,
    )

In the older version, width can be negative, while height must still be positive. You can also pass the function or Dimensions.check_width, but when one function backs several validators, as must_be_positive does here, Cadwyn raises CadwynStructureError and asks for the name.

docs.title: Rename a schema in the older version
docs.text:
The following code replaces all schema name occurrences with a new one to ensure that the name is different in openapi.json:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema


class RenameOtherSchemaToMySchema(VersionChange):
    """'OtherSchema' has been renamed to 'MySchema' to match the resource name
    used throughout the API.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(MySchema).had(name="OtherSchema"),
    )

docs.title: Change model configuration in the older version
docs.text:
Pass config=ConfigDict(...) to schema(Model).had(...) to patch selected Pydantic config keys. Keys you omit keep their current values. The supported keys are extra, populate_by_name, validate_by_alias, validate_by_name, str_strip_whitespace, frozen, title, json_schema_extra, and arbitrary_types_allowed.

For example, this older API forbids extra fields and has no nickname field:

from cadwyn import (
    Cadwyn,
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    Version,
    VersionBundle,
    VersionChange,
    VersionedAPIRouter,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict


class User(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="allow")
    name: str
    nickname: str = "anonymous"


class AllowExtraUserFields(VersionChange):
    """User requests and responses now allow extra fields."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(User).had(config=ConfigDict(extra="forbid")),
        schema(User).field("nickname").didnt_exist,
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(User)
    def supply_nickname(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["nickname"] = request.body["name"]

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(User)
    def remove_newer_keys(response: ResponseInfo):
        del response.body["nickname"]
        del response.body["server_note"]


router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.post("/users")
def create_user(user: User) -> User:
    return User.model_validate(user.model_dump() | {"server_note": "created"})


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(
        Version("2001-01-01", AllowExtraUserFields),
        Version("2000-01-01"),
    ),
)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

Request validation uses the client's config before request migrations. Sending {"name": "Alice", "nickname": "Al"} to the older version returns a 422, so a request migration cannot remove an unknown key to make it acceptable. Sending only {"name": "Alice"} succeeds: the request migration supplies the nickname for HEAD. Responses migrate before validation with the client's config. The response migration above removes nickname and server_note so the older version returns {"name": "Alice"}. Cadwyn never silently removes these keys for you; without the response migration, older response validation fails.

Config instructions only support leaf models. If a model has subclasses among the app's versioned models, an instruction changing its config fails at startup. Put the config instruction on each subclass (leaf model) instead. Pydantic stores merged configs without recording whether each setting was inherited or explicitly overridden, so Cadwyn cannot safely propagate a parent's config change. An instruction on a leaf subclass leaves its parent and siblings unchanged; unused subclasses elsewhere in your code do not prevent it.

Generic parametrizations such as Bag[Item] and Cadwyn's generated copies do not count as user subclasses. A config patch on Bag also applies to its parametrizations, including the specialization used when a route accepts bare Bag. An instruction on a particular parametrization can override those keys for that parametrization alone. A declared subclass such as class SpecialBag(Bag[Item]) still counts as a subclass and prevents config instructions on Bag.

Changing populate_by_name also sets validate_by_alias=True and validate_by_name to its older value. Explicit validate_by_alias and validate_by_name entries in the same patch take precedence. To change those flags individually, patch them directly. At least one must remain enabled, as in Pydantic.

There is no config didnt_have instruction: set the older value explicitly, such as ConfigDict(frozen=False) or ConfigDict(json_schema_extra=None). Cadwyn rejects a key whose value is already the current value, including an implicit Pydantic default. An empty patch on its own is also rejected.

Unknown and unsupported keys fail when the instruction is declared, with an error naming the model and key. In particular, aliases and field titles already stored on fields cannot be regenerated safely with alias_generator or field_title_generator. Model construction hooks (model_title_generator, schema_generator, and plugin_settings), attribute classification (ignored_types and protected_namespaces), use_attribute_docstrings, and defer_build cannot be versioned either. Config keys outside the supported list remain unchanged across versions. Enabling arbitrary_types_allowed permits arbitrary Python instances, but those types still need their own JSON schema support to appear in OpenAPI, as in Pydantic.

You can combine config=, name=, and description= in one instruction. cadwyn render includes changed model configs. Apps without config instructions keep their existing behavior and OpenAPI.

docs.title: Change the description of a schema in the older version
docs.text:
Pydantic uses the docstring of a schema as its description in openapi.json, and Cadwyn copies it into every version of the schema. Use had(description=...) to give the older versions a different description:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    """A user of the API who can belong to several organizations."""

    name: str


class AllowUsersToBelongToSeveralOrganizations(VersionChange):
    """Users can now belong to several organizations."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(User).had(
            description="A user of the API who belongs to one organization."
        ),
    )

Pass description=None to remove the description from the older versions. Cadwyn rejects blank descriptions such as " ". You can also pass name and description together, e.g. schema(User).had(name="OldUser", description="An old user.").

Like name, the description only applies to the schema itself, not to its subclasses: like in pydantic, every schema has its own docstring. For the same reason, the description of a generic schema such as Page does not show up for its parametrizations such as Page[Item], which have no description in pydantic. Like other instructions, the description of a model in the type args of a generic, such as Item in Page[Item], also changes there (see Generic models). If the schema sets json_schema_extra={"description": ...} in its model_config, that description overrides the docstring in every version.

The latest version keeps the docstring from your code, so if the docstring contains internal notes that no version should show, put the public description into HeadVersion, which applies it to every version, including the latest one:

from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle, VersionChange, schema


class HideInternalNotesOfUser(VersionChange):
    description = "Hide the internal notes of 'User' from the API reference"
    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(User).had(description="A user of the API."),
    )


versions = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(HideInternalNotesOfUser),
    Version("2001-01-01"),
)

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
As Cadwyn allows to keep the same business logic, database schemas, etc., you can maintain a single set of common tests for the current latest version. These tests work like regular tests that you would have without API versioning.

Here's a suggested structure for test files:

└── tests
    ├── __init__.py
    ├── conftest.py
    ├── head
    │   ├── __init__.py
    │   ├── conftest.py
    │   ├── test_users.py
    │   ├── test_admins.py
    │   └── test_invoices.py
    ├── v2022_11_16
    │   ├── __init__.py
    │   ├── conftest.py
    │   └── test_invoices.py
    └── v2023_03_11
        ├── __init__.py
        ├── conftest.py
        └── test_users.py

The following process is recommended when creating a new version:

  1. Before creating a new version, apply the changes you want to your logic and schemas in the latest version (i.e., introduce the intended breaking changes), and then run the tests in the head directory. The failing tests will indicate the broken contracts
  2. Create a new subdirectory in tests, name it after the previous version (e.g., v2024_05_04), and copy only the failing tests into it. Ensure that these tests invoke the old version of the API
  3. Write a VersionChange that fixes the tests in this previous version using converters. In the new version, those same tests should still fail
  4. Modify the tests in the head directory so that they validate the new API contract and pass successfully

This approach helps to keep old versions covered by tests while minimizing test code duplication.

docs.title: Version Changes
docs.text:
Version changes are the backbone of Cadwyn. They allow to describe things like "this field in that schema had a different name in an older version" or "this endpoint did not exist in all earlier versions".

In Cadwyn, your business logic always works with a single version: HEAD, which represents your latest version. This approach decouples your business logic from versioning and allows you to support hundreds of API versions using the same database models and business logic, while staying sane.

Follow these steps to add a new version:

  1. Introduce a breaking change in your HEAD version
  2. Apply reverse changes to older versions using special "migration instructions" so that your current users are not affected by the breaking changes

Migration instructions for reverting breaking changes should be grouped to simplify maintenance efforts. For example, renaming the creation_date field to created_at and deleting the GET /v1/tax_ids endpoint are unrelated changes and should be placed in separate groups. In contrast, deleting the POST /v1/tax_ids endpoint should be grouped with deleting the GET /v1/tax_ids. Such grouping makes the changes easier to understand for both your users and developers.

Each such group is called a version change:

# versions/v2023_02_10.py

from cadwyn import VersionChange, endpoint


class RemoveTaxIdEndpoints(VersionChange):
    """The 'GET /v1/tax_ids' and 'POST /v1/tax_ids' endpoints have been
    removed because tax IDs are now managed on customer records.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        endpoint("/v1/tax_ids", ["GET", "POST"]).existed,
    )

After describing the groups, add your version change class(es) to your version bundle to activate them:

# versions/__init__.py

from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2023_02_10 import RemoveTaxIdEndpoints

versions = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(),
    Version("2023-02-10", RemoveTaxIdEndpoints),
    Version("2022-11-16"),
)

This instructs Cadwyn to undelete these endpoints in all versions before 2023-02-10.

The following explains what each part does and why:

docs.title: VersionBundle
docs.text:
VersionBundle is the single source of truth for your list of versions. It stores all versions and all version changes associated with them. Each version change represents a group of breaking changes. Each Version contains a group of version changes that led to its creation. For example, if you delete the POST /v1/tax_ids endpoint in version 2023-02-10, you need to add a corresponding version change to the 2023-02-10 version. For example:

# versions/__init__.py

from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2023_02_10 import RemoveTaxIdEndpoints

versions = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(),
    Version("2023-02-10", RemoveTaxIdEndpoints),
    Version("2022-11-16"),
)

Did you notice that the initial 2022-11-16 version has no version changes? That is intentional. How could it have breaking changes if there were no prior versions?

docs.title: Version
docs.text: Version is an ordered collection of version changes that describes when each version change occurred allowing Cadwyn to generate schemas and routes for all versions correctly, based on which version changes belong to which versions.

docs.title: HeadVersion
docs.text:
Cadwyn has a special HEAD version: it is the only version you will create manually and use directly in your business logic. Cadwyn generates all other versions from HEAD version.
