When handling an HTTP request, Cadwyn first validates it against the requested API version. Then all the converters from the requested API version up to the latest API version are applied to it. Finally, Cadwyn converts the request to the requested schema from HEAD version (the schema that was used to generate the versioned schema from the requested API version).

So Cadwyn migrates all requests from all versions to HEAD version to ensure that your business logic operates on a single version.

HEAD is very similar to your latest version but for a few key differences:

  • Latest is user-facing while HEAD is only used internally by you and Cadwyn
  • Latest is generated while HEAD is maintained by you manually
  • Latest includes only the fields that API user is supposed to see while HEAD may include some fields missing from latest. For example, if an earlier version contained a field completely incompatible with latest, HEAD will still include it to ensure that older versions continue to function as before. This also applies to field types: if a field is required in latest but was nullable in an earlier version, then HEAD will keep it nullable to ensure that earlier version requests can easily be converted into HEAD requests
  • Latest may include constraints that are incompatible with older versions while HEAD may contain none. If you prefer, the user-facing schemas are applied for validation before the request is converted to HEAD so HEAD does not need to re-validate anything if you do not want it to

docs.title: VersionChange
docs.text:
VersionChange classes describe each atomic group of business capabilities that you have altered in a version.

Note, however, that a migration is required only if it is a breaking change for your users. If you add a new endpoint or a new field to your response schema, you do not need a migration because it will not break your users’ code. If you do not create a migration, this change is automatically added to all versions.

docs.title: VersionChange.__name__
docs.text:
The name of a version change should clearly describe the breaking change it introduces. For example, RemoveTaxIdEndpoints immediately communicates what has changed. The name should begin with a verb and serve as the primary clue for developers unfamiliar with the history of the project to understand the difference between versions. Do not hesitate to use long, descriptive names. It is better to choose a verbose name that precisely conveys the change than a short, generic one. For example RenameCreationDatetimeAndUpdateDatetimeToCreatedAtAndUpdatedAt is far more informative than RefactorFields. After only a few poorly named version changes, the entire versioning history can become difficult to read and understand:

versions = VersionBundle(
    Version("2023-05-09", ChangeCreateLogic, AddRequiredFields),
    Version("2023-04-02", DeleteEndpoint, ChangeFields, RenameFields),
    Version("2023-02-10", RenameEndpoints, RefactorFields),
    Version("2022-11-16"),
)

docs.title: VersionChange.description
docs.text:
Write the description of your version change as its class docstring. Cadwyn uses this docstring as the description of the version change.

The description should clearly communicate to your clients what happened and why. Make it grammatically correct, detailed, specific, and written for humans. Note that you do not have to use a strict machine-readable format: it is a piece of documentation, not a set of instructions. As a reference, consider the following version change description from Stripe:

Event objects (and webhooks) will now render a `request` subobject that contains a request Id and idempotency key instead of a string request Id.

It is concise, descriptive, and human-readable — qualities of effective technical documentation. Now compare it with a less helpful description:

Migration from the first version (2022-11-16) to 2023-09-01 version.
Changes:
* Changed schema for `POST /v1/tax_ids` endpoint
  • Its first line, Migration from the first version (2022-11-16) to 2023-09-01 version., duplicates the already-known information. Your developers can determine which version VersionChange migrates to and from by its location in VersionBundle and most likely by its file name. So it is redundant information
  • Its second line, Changes:, does not provide useful information either because a description of a VersionChange cannot describe anything but changes. So again, it is redundant information
  • Its third line, Changed schema for 'POST /v1/tax_ids' endpoint, provides both too much and too little information. It states that a schema was changed but it does not specify what was changed. The goal is to make it easy for your clients to migrate from one version to the next. A more useful description would mention the OpenAPI model name that was changed, the fields that were modified, and the reason for those changes

docs.title: VersionChange.instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version
docs.text:
In Cadwyn, you use the latest version. This attribute allows you to describe how your schemas and endpoints looked in previous versions. Cadwyn uses this information to determine how to generate the schemas and routes to recreate the previous schemas and endpoints for your clients. So you only need to maintain your head (latest) schemas and your migrations while Cadwyn handles the rest. In fact, you put minimal effort into maintaining your migrations because they are effectively immutable records of the breaking changes that happened in the past. Once written, they do not need to be modified.

This approach of maintaining the present and describing the past may seem counterintuitive at first. The key is to adopt the correct mindset. After one or two attempts at versioning you will see how much sense this approach makes.

Suppose you need to know what your code looked like two weeks ago. You would use git checkout or git reset to jump to an older commit because Git stores the latest version of your code (referred to as HEAD) and the diffs between it and each previous version as a chain of changes. Cadwyn works the same way: Cadwyn stores only the latest version and regenerates previous versions on demand using diffs.

Note for curious readers Git doesn't actually work this way internally. The description above is closer to how SVN works. It is just a simple metaphor to explain a concept.

docs.title: Data migrations
docs.text:
Consider a scenario where you rename the creation_date field to created_at. You have updated your schemas — that's great! However, clients using previous versions of the API will continue to send requests containing creation_date instead of created_at. How do you handle this? Well, in Cadwyn your business logic never receives requests from the previous versions. Instead, it receives only the requests of the latest version. So whenever you define a version change that renames a field, you also need to specify how to convert the request body from the previous version to the new one. For example:

from cadwyn import (
    RequestInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    schema,
)
from invoices import InvoiceCreateRequest


class RenameInvoiceCreationDateToCreatedAt(VersionChange):
    """Invoice creation timestamps are now returned as 'created_at' instead of
    'creation_date' to align with the API's other timestamp fields.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(InvoiceCreateRequest)
        .field("created_at")
        .had(name="creation_date"),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(InvoiceCreateRequest)
    def rename_creation_date_to_created_at(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["created_at"] = request.body.pop("creation_date")

Did you notice how the schema for InvoiceCreateRequest is specified in the migration above? This instructs Cadwyn to apply it to all routes that use this schema as their request body.

At this point, you have described not only how the schemas have changed, but also how to migrate a request from the previous version to the new one. When Cadwyn receives a request targeting a specific API version, it first validates the request against the schema for that version. Then Cadwyn applies each request migration in sequence up to the latest version. As a result, your business logic always receives the latest version of the request, while from your clients’ perspective, multiple API versions are available. Cadwyn allows you to support versioned APIs without adding complexity to your business logic.

If the body is a list or a dict of schemas, such as list[InvoiceCreateRequest], or a tuple or a set of them, request.body holds the instances of the schemas of the client's version instead of dicts. A migration can change their attributes or replace them with dicts. After the migrations, Cadwyn passes the fields that are set and the extra keys of the instances in lists and dicts to the latest version, so it gets what the client has sent, as long as Cadwyn can be sure that it's right (see the known limitations).

Computed fields are left out of model request bodies, including nested models: migrations that need their values must compute them, and endpoints should not expect them in model_extra. Models that override model_dump() keep their previous dumping behavior (see known limitations).

Cadwyn follows FastAPI's strict_content_type setting when reading bodies. Send Content-Type: application/json for JSON; without it, migrations may receive raw bytes rather than a dict. To accept JSON without that header, set strict_content_type=False on the app, router, or route.

If Cadwyn restores validation aliases before validating the latest request, it solves the latest dependencies once and reports that restored body's errors in CadwynHeadRequestValidationError. A field with a default supplied only by a custom core schema no longer falls back to that default for a rejected value: remove the value in a request migration if that fallback is intended.

A request migration can also remove a body that is not a form: if it sets request.body = None, the latest version gets the request without a body, so the defaults of its body params apply. If no migration assigns request.body, an omitted body stays omitted, and on FastAPI 0.151.0 and newer, a JSON null body stays null.

But wait... What happens to the Invoice responses? Your business logic now returns created_at, which means clients using previous API versions will be affected. Cadwyn solves this as well by allowing you to define response migrations. Requests are migrated forward in versions while responses are migrated backward in versions. In other words, your business logic returns a response of the latest version and Cadwyn will use your response migrations to migrate the response back to the version of your client's request:

from cadwyn import (
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from invoices import (
    BaseInvoice,
    InvoiceCreateRequest,
    InvoiceResource,
)


class RenameInvoiceCreationDateToCreatedAt(VersionChange):
    """Invoice creation timestamps are now returned as 'created_at' instead of
    'creation_date' to align with the API's other timestamp fields.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseInvoice).field("created_at").had(name="creation_date"),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(InvoiceCreateRequest)
    def rename_creation_date_to_created_at(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["created_at"] = request.body.pop("creation_date")

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(InvoiceResource)
    def rename_created_at_to_creation_date(response: ResponseInfo):
        response.body["creation_date"] = response.body.pop("created_at")

Did you notice how the schema for InvoiceResource is specified in the migration above? This instructs Cadwyn to apply it to all routes with this schema as their response_model. Also notice that BaseInvoice is now used in the instructions. Here, BaseInvoice is the parent of both InvoiceCreateRequest and InvoiceResource, so renaming it in the instructions will rename the field in those schemas as well. Rename an inherited field in the parent like this. Renaming it only in a child schema fails at startup, because the child would still inherit the old field from its parent. If a child schema changed the field in a newer version or declares it again, rename it in that child and in the parent in the same version. Otherwise, Cadwyn fails at startup too, because the child would keep the old field next to the renamed one.

Migrations only run for the schema you name

Instructions such as schema(InvoiceResource).field(...).had(...) change the schema everywhere it is used, including inside other schemas and generics. Request and response migrations are different: a schema-based migration only runs when its schema is the request body or the response_model of the route itself. It does not run for that schema nested in another one, e.g. in a field of another schema or inside a generic such as Page[InvoiceResource], so write the migration for the outer schema instead. This is a deliberate choice: each migration runs exactly where you declared it and never twice for the same data.

Unions of schemas

If the request body or the response_model is a union that has the schema as a member, e.g. Union[InvoiceResource, RefundResource] or Optional[InvoiceResource], the migration runs only for the requests and responses that are that member. For requests, that's the member that the body of the client's version validates into. For responses, it's the member whose model the endpoint returns an object of, so an object of a subclass of the schema, such as an internal representation, counts as the schema, and None is no member. A migration declared for the union itself (convert_response_to_previous_version_for(Union[InvoiceResource, RefundResource])) replaces the migrations of its members in the same version change. Annotated and named type aliases (TypeAliasType("Resource", Union[InvoiceResource, RefundResource])) mean the same as their value.

If Cadwyn can't tell which member a request or a response is, it fails with a CadwynError instead of guessing, but only if a migration of a member would run:

  • The endpoint returns something else than an object of a member's model or None, e.g. a dict or a database object. Cadwyn could only find out which member it becomes by validating it, which would run its validators twice, because FastAPI validates it again with the models of the client's version after the migrations. Return an object of the member's model, or migrate the endpoint by its path.
  • The endpoint returns a Response object, such as a JSONResponse, which FastAPI doesn't validate. Return an object of the member's model instead (e.g. InvoiceResource(...), not the dict that you put in the JSONResponse), or migrate the endpoint by its path.
  • The response or the body is an object of several members that don't inherit from each other (e.g. class Both(InvoiceResource, RefundResource)). Use an object of only one of them, or migrate the endpoint by its path.
  • The request body param has an alias (Body(alias=...)), so the endpoint doesn't get the body under the name that Cadwyn looks it up by. Remove the alias, or migrate the endpoint by its path.

A migration of a member with migrate_http_errors=True fails at startup with a RouterGenerationError if a union route exists in a version that it migrates, because an error isn't any member of the union. Migrate the errors of the endpoint by its path instead.

When a request comes in, Cadwyn migrates it to the latest version using the request migration. You then handle your business logic, return the latest response, and Cadwyn migrates it back to the requested API version. Does your business logic or database know that you have two versions? No, not at all. It is zero-cost. Consider the benefits of supporting not just two, but two hundred versions.

Did you notice how the latest versions of the schemas are used in the migration above? Such pattern can be found everywhere in Cadwyn. The latest version of your schemas is used to describe what happened to all other versions because other versions might not exist when you are defining migrations for them.

docs.title: Path-based migration specification
docs.text:
Often you need to migrate based on the endpoint path rather than the request body or response model. This happens when, for example, an endpoint does not have a request body, or its response model is used in other places that you do not want to migrate. Consider the example above, but use paths instead of schemas:

from cadwyn import (
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from invoices import BaseInvoice


class RenameInvoiceCreationDateToCreatedAt(VersionChange):
    """Invoice creation timestamps are now returned as 'created_at' instead of
    'creation_date' to align with the API's other timestamp fields.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseInvoice).field("created_at").had(name="creation_date"),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for("/v1/invoices", ["POST"])
    def rename_creation_date_to_created_at(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["created_at"] = request.body.pop("creation_date")

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for("/v1/invoices", ["GET"])
    def rename_created_at_to_creation_date(response: ResponseInfo):
        response.body["creation_date"] = response.body.pop("created_at")

That said, schemas are highly recommended, since it is much easier to introduce inconsistencies when using paths. For example, if you have ten endpoints sharing the same response body schema, you might forget to add migrations for three of them because you are using paths instead of schemas.

docs.title: Migration of HTTP errors
docs.text:
Often you need to raise fastapi.HTTPException in your code to signal an error to your users. However, changing the status code of an error would be a breaking change because your error status codes - and sometimes even the response bodies - are part of your API contract.

By default, Cadwyn's response migrations do not handle errors, but you can enable error handling with the migrate_http_errors keyword argument:

from cadwyn import (
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
)


class ReplaceInvoiceNotFoundStatusCode400With404(VersionChange):
    """Missing invoices from 'GET /v1/invoices' now return 404 instead of 400
    so clients can distinguish absent resources from invalid requests.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = ()

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(
        "/v1/invoices", ["GET"], migrate_http_errors=True
    )
    def replace_404_with_400(response: ResponseInfo):
        if response.status_code == 404:
            response.status_code = 400

docs.title: Migration of non-body attributes
docs.text:
Cadwyn can migrate more than just request bodies.

RequestInfo has the following interfaces to migrate requests:

  • body: Any
  • headers: starlette.datastructures.MutableHeaders
  • cookies: dict[str, str]
  • query_params: dict[str, str]
  • form: list[tuple[str, UploadFile | str]] | None for requests to endpoints that declare their form fields as separate Form() or File() parameters. Otherwise it is None. For example, an endpoint that takes a single model through Form() gets the model's fields as a dict in body instead

If a migration reads an uploaded file from form, it must seek the file back to where the latest version should start reading it, usually upload.file.seek(0). Otherwise, the latest version gets the file as the migration left it, e.g. empty.

Uploads of versioned routes remain open through background tasks, including uploads that migrations add and later replace or remove. Once the versioned endpoint starts, Cadwyn shields cleanup from cancellation, gives each upload three seconds to close, and logs a warning on timeout; cancellation before that point and unversioned routes depend on FastAPI's cleanup.

ResponseInfo has the following interfaces to migrate responses:

  • body: Any
  • status_code: int
  • headers: starlette.datastructures.MutableHeaders
  • set_cookie
  • delete_cookie

docs.title: Internal representations
docs.text:
So far, only simple cases have been considered. But what happens if you cannot migrate your data that easily? This can happen if your earlier versions stored more data than your newer versions. Or if they supported more data formats.

Suppose the User schema previously had a list of addresses, but now you want to make a breaking change and replace addresses with a single address. A naive migration would take the first address from the list in each request and convert that address into a list in each response as follows:

from cadwyn import (
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from users import BaseUser


# AN EXAMPLE OF A POOR MIGRATION
class ReplaceUserAddressesWithAddress(VersionChange):
    """Users now expose a single 'address' instead of 'addresses' because only
    one mailing address is supported.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser).field("address").didnt_exist,
        schema(BaseUser).field("addresses").existed_as(type=list[str]),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(BaseUser)
    def turn_addresses_into_a_single_item(request: RequestInfo):
        addresses = request.body.pop("addresses")
        # The list might have been empty previously so new 'address'
        # field must be nullable.
        request.body["address"] = addresses[0] if addresses else None

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(BaseUser)
    def turn_address_into_a_list(response: ResponseInfo):
        response.body["addresses"] = [response.body.pop("address")]

But this will not work. If the user of the previous version requests to save three addresses, only one will actually be saved. Existing data is also going to be affected: if old users had multiple addresses, only one of them will be returned. This is important: a breaking change has been introduced.

In order to solve this issue, Cadwyn uses a concept of internal representations. An internal representation of your data is like a database entry for your data — it consists of its latest version plus all the fields that are incompatible with the latest API version. If the discussion were about classes, then internal representation would be a child of your latest schemas - it has all the same data and a little more, expanding its functionality. Your internal representation of user object can contain much more data than your latest schemas.

So all your requests get migrated to HEAD, which is the internal representation of latest, rather than the latest itself. Its data is very similar to that of latest. The same applies to your responses: instead of responding with and migrating from the latest version of your data, you use its internal representation which is pretty similar to the actual latest schemas.

For responses, returning the internal representation is simple: return your database model or a dictionary with everything you need for all your versions. In the user address example, it is recommended to continue storing the list of addresses in the database and include a single address in a response. The latest schemas will strip it while previous schemas will be able to use it.

# in your business logic
@router.get("/users/{user_id}", response_model=User)
async def get_user(user_id: int):
    user = database[user_id]
    return {
        "address": user.addresses[0] if user.addresses else None,
        **user.model_dump(),
    }

So now your migration will look like the following:

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from users import User


class ReplaceUserAddressesWithAddress(VersionChange):
    """Users now expose a single 'address' instead of 'addresses' because only
    one mailing address is supported.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(User).field("address").didnt_exist,
        schema(User).field("addresses").existed_as(type=list[str]),
    )

Yes, you no longer need any of the migrations because responses are handled automatically. See the how-to section for an example of how to achieve the same result with requests.

docs.title: Manual body migrations
docs.text:
Often you will need to migrate your data outside of routing, manually. For example, you might need to send a versioned response to your client via a webhook or inside a worker/cronjob. In these cases, use cadwyn.schema_generation.migrate_response_body():

from cadwyn.schema_generation import migrate_response_body
from users import UserResource
from versions import versions

body_from_2000_01_01 = migrate_response_body(
    versions, UserResource, latest_body={"name": "John"}, version="2000-01-01"
)

The returned body_from_2000_01_01 is your data passed through all converters (as it would be when returned from your route) and wrapped in the 2000-01-01 version of UserResource. Because the data is wrapped, you can include Pydantic’s defaults.

Like route responses, migrate_response_body() restores validation aliases only when missing keys would certainly fail validation, such as required fields or forbidden extras. In other cases, make migrations set validation keys explicitly, e.g. v for Field(alias="x", validation_alias="v"). Restored bodies are validated once and report their own errors; aliased fields whose defaults come only from custom core schemas keep supplied values or reject invalid ones instead of silently using defaults. To request the default, delete the value in a response migration, or from latest_body before calling migrate_response_body().

docs.title: StreamingResponse and FileResponse migrations
docs.text: Migrations for the bodies of fastapi.responses.StreamingResponse and fastapi.responses.FileResponse are not directly supported yet (1, 2). However, you can use ResponseInfo._response attribute to get access to the original StreamingResponse or FileResponse and modify it as needed within your migrations.

docs.title: Pydantic RootModel migration warning
docs.text:
Pydantic has an implementation detail: pydantic.RootModel instances are memoized. So the following code is going to output True:

from pydantic import RootModel
from users import User

BulkCreateUsersRequestBody = RootModel[list[User]]
BulkCreateUsersResponseBody = RootModel[list[User]]

print(BulkCreateUsersRequestBody is BulkCreateUsersResponseBody)  # True

A migration intended for one of these schemas will affect both. A recommended alternative is to either use subclassing:

from pydantic import RootModel
from users import User

UserList = RootModel[list[User]]


class BulkCreateUsersRequestBody(UserList):
    pass


class BulkCreateUsersResponseBody(UserList):
    pass


print(BulkCreateUsersRequestBody is BulkCreateUsersResponseBody)  # False

or to specify migrations using endpoint path instead of a schema.

docs.title: Dependency re-execution warning
docs.text:
Notice that whenever a request reaches Cadwyn, it is first validated against the request's version of the schema, then it is migrated to the latest version, and then validated again to prevent migrations from creating invalid requests.

This means that if you have a dependency that is executed during the request validation, it will be executed twice. For example, if you have a dependency that checks whether a user exists in the database, it will be executed twice. This is not an issue if the dependency is idempotent, but it becomes one if it is not.

To solve this issue, you can use the cadwyn.current_dependency_solver dependency which tells you whether your dependency is called before or after the request is migrated. If you want to run it after Cadwyn has migrated the request to the latest version, ensure that current_dependency_solver is set to "cadwyn". If you want your dependency to run at the very beginning of handling the request, you should run it when current_dependency_solver is "fastapi".

from typing import Annotated, Literal

from cadwyn import current_dependency_solver
from fastapi import Depends


def my_dependency(
    dependency_solver: Annotated[
        Literal["fastapi", "cadwyn"], Depends(current_dependency_solver)
    ],
):
    if dependency_solver == "fastapi":  # Before migration
        ...
    else:  # After migration
        ...

but the majority of your dependencies will not need this as most dependencies should not have side effects or network calls within them.

Dependencies that read uploaded files or move their position (e.g. to skip a header) need care: both runs see the same files. Do such work in the run that gives your endpoint its arguments, i.e. when current_dependency_solver is "cadwyn", or "fastapi" for requests that Cadwyn doesn't migrate (requests without an API version). Before the "cadwyn" run, Cadwyn moves the files that FastAPI has read for bytes params back to their start, so a file that a dependency has moved only in the "fastapi" run can be moved back.

docs.title: Background tasks added by dependencies
docs.text:
Background tasks that a dependency adds are side effects too. FastAPI runs the tasks that dependencies add in the first run after the response. In the second run, Cadwyn keeps them only if the endpoint itself declares a BackgroundTasks param. Otherwise, it drops them and emits a FutureWarning once per route:

  • Cadwyn warns after FastAPI has sent the response and run its background tasks, i.e. when the dropped tasks would have run. Requests that fail, and responses that have their own background tasks (e.g. JSONResponse(..., background=...)), don't warn, because FastAPI wouldn't run the dropped tasks for them either
  • Cadwyn decides whether to warn when the endpoint returns. Tasks that a dependency adds only after that, e.g. after the yield of a dependency with scope="function", are dropped without a warning
  • Cadwyn warns in a worker thread, so slow log handlers don't block the event loop. If your warning filters turn the warning into an error, Cadwyn logs it instead. If logging fails too, Cadwyn ignores the error. The response and the other background tasks are never affected

Cadwyn 10.0 will always run these tasks. To run them now, pass run_background_tasks_of_latest_version_dependencies=True to Cadwyn() or generate_versioned_routers(). Then every task that a dependency adds runs once after the response, in the order it was added, as in FastAPI. As in FastAPI, a response that has its own background tasks runs only them. To give the second run the background tasks that FastAPI runs, Cadwyn adds a BackgroundTasks param to the endpoints that don't declare one. It's named cadwyn_background_tasks_param, with trailing underscores if the endpoint already has a param with that name. You can see it in the signature of the route's endpoint and in route.dependant.background_tasks_param_name, but not in OpenAPI, and the endpoint doesn't get it.

A dependency that adds a task in both runs then has it run twice, so add the task in only one of the runs. The "fastapi" run happens for every request, including the ones that Cadwyn doesn't migrate:

from typing import Annotated, Literal

from cadwyn import (
    Cadwyn,
    Version,
    VersionBundle,
    VersionedAPIRouter,
    current_dependency_solver,
)
from fastapi import BackgroundTasks, Depends

sent_emails: list[str] = []


def send_welcome_email(email: str) -> None:
    sent_emails.append(email)


def schedule_welcome_email(
    email: str,
    background_tasks: BackgroundTasks,
    dependency_solver: Annotated[
        Literal["fastapi", "cadwyn"], Depends(current_dependency_solver)
    ],
):
    # Dependencies run twice, so we add the task in only one of the runs
    if dependency_solver == "fastapi":
        background_tasks.add_task(send_welcome_email, email)


router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.post("/users", dependencies=[Depends(schedule_welcome_email)])
async def create_user():
    return {}


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(Version("2023-02-10"), Version("2022-11-16")),
    run_background_tasks_of_latest_version_dependencies=True,
)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

docs.title: Versioned dependencies
docs.text:
In the first run, Cadwyn can give a dependency its version's copy, whose parameters (request bodies, query parameters, and so on) are validated and documented in OpenAPI with the request's version of their models and enums. Whether it does depends on how you declare the dependency:

  • value: T = Depends(f): every version, including the latest one, uses its copy of f.
  • value: Annotated[T, Depends(f)] (or Security(f), or Annotated[f, Depends()]): a version uses its copy of f if the models or enums that the parameters of f validate have instructions in a newer version or in HeadVersion. This includes the models and enums in sub-dependencies, in the types of the fields of models, and in the typed extra fields of models that allow them (__pydantic_extra__). It also includes the models whose bases have such instructions, unless these instructions only change fields that the model overrides without renaming them. It doesn't include what pydantic doesn't validate: class variables, default factories, fields that a subclass overrides, the type args of generic models that no field uses, and the args of generic type aliases that their values don't use (e.g. Unused[Role] with type Unused[T] = str), also behind other type aliases and in the parameters of f. In a type alias that refers to itself, such as type Tree[T] = str | list[Tree[T]], the references to itself with the same args add nothing, so Tree[Role] doesn't count Role, while references with other args count their args. An alias that Cadwyn cannot expand (e.g. with a TypeVarTuple) counts all of its args. So the latest version uses its copy only if HeadVersion has such instructions. Other versions usually use f itself, with the latest models and enums, except where they already used copies before: when T refers to Pydantic models (Cadwyn copies them for every version) or to enums with instructions, when the other Annotated metadata cannot be hashed (e.g. Security(f, scopes=[...])), when Python's typing cache no longer holds the original Annotated[...] (it keeps a limited number of them, so in apps with many Annotated dependencies this can apply to every version; such copies use the same unversioned classes, so they behave the same), and for Annotated[f, Depends()], which can already give f copies of the models and enums that its parameters use.
  • Pydantic models used as dependencies, such as Depends(Filters), are copied for every version in both forms, as before. Other classes, such as Depends(RoleChecker), are not versioned: the parameters of their __init__ use the latest models and enums in every version.

Where a version uses its copy of a dependency, the dependency receives that version's copies of the models and enums in the first run, not the classes themselves. So isinstance(item, Item), role is Role.admin, == between the members of a plain Enum, and dicts keyed by enum members do not match them. Compare by value instead (e.g. role.value == "admin"), or do such work only when current_dependency_solver is "cadwyn", where the dependency gets the latest classes. On FastAPI versions before 0.148, a default that is an enum member, such as role: Role = Query(Role.reader) for a query, header, cookie, or form parameter, can also make requests that omit the parameter fail with a 422 when the version removes the member or changes its value.

docs.title: Version changes with side effects
docs.text:
Sometimes you will use API versioning to handle a breaking change in your business logic, not in the schemas themselves. In such cases, it is tempting to add a version check and follow the new business logic such as:

# This is wrong. Please do not do this.
if api_version_var.get() >= date(2022, 11, 11):
    # do new logic here
    ...

Instead, Cadwyn provides a special VersionChangeWithSideEffects class for handling such cases. It makes finding dangerous versions that have side effects much easier and provides a nice abstraction for checking whether you are on a version where these side effects have been applied.

As an example, let's use the tutorial section's case with the user and their address. Suppose you use an external service to check whether user's address is listed in it and return 400 response if it is not. Also suppose that you have only added this check in the newest version.

from cadwyn import VersionChangeWithSideEffects


class RejectUserAddressesMissingFromExternalService(
    VersionChangeWithSideEffects
):
    """User addresses are now verified by an external service during creation;
    invalid addresses return 400 to prevent storing undeliverable locations.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = ()

Then you will have the following check in your business logic:

from src.versions import RejectUserAddressesMissingFromExternalService


async def create_user(payload):
    if RejectUserAddressesMissingFromExternalService.is_applied:
        check_user_address_exists_in_an_external_service(payload.address)
    ...

So this change can be contained in any version. Your business logic doesn't know which version it has. And shouldn't.

docs.title: Warning against side effects
docs.text:
Side effects are a very powerful tool but they must be used with great caution. Are you sure you MUST change your business logic? Are you sure what you are trying to do cannot just be done by a migration? 90% of time, you will not need them. Please think twice before using them. API versioning is about having the same underlying app and data while changing the schemas and API endpoints to interact with it. By introducing side effects, you leak versioning into your business logic and possibly even your data which makes your code significantly harder to maintain in the long term. If each side effect adds a single if statement to your logic, then after 100 versions with side effects, you will have 100 additional if statements. If used correctly, Cadwyn helps you maintain decades’ worth of API versions with minimal maintenance effort, and side effects make it significantly harder to do. Changes in the underlying source, structure, or logic of your data should not affect your API or public-facing business logic.

However, the following use cases often necessitate side effects.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file. Please follow the Keep a Changelog standard.

docs.title: Breaking
docs.text:
• cadwyn render now handles NamedTuple and defaultdict defaults and preserves Counter counts and nested default expressions. Unsafe recursive/shared defaults, subclass representations that lose their type, and unsupported mapping state or factories now raise CadwynRenderError; use a named Field(default_factory=...) function for these defaults (#590). Nonfinite floats now render as executable float(...) calls instead of unbound inf and nan names.
  • Models with safely resolvable __mro_entries__ bases now inherit versioned parents affected by schema instructions and their inherited-field startup checks (#588). Update affected request and response migrations for corrected older-version fields, and fix conflicting rename or deletion instructions in the declaring models. Dynamically resolved, incomplete, or unmatched bases retain their previous behavior.
  • Bare generic models and unparametrized type aliases now version the models and enums used by TypeVar bounds, constraints, and defaults, so older versions reject latest-only shapes and affected generic OpenAPI names may change (#584). Add migrations for the outer generic or endpoint where nested data changes; unsafe fallbacks raise SchemaGenerationError, so use explicit type arguments. TypeVar-based typed extra fields remain a known limitation; use concrete model annotations there.
  • Cadwyn now requires Python 3.11+ and Pydantic 2.12.0+ (#570). Upgrade them, or stay on Cadwyn 8.x.
  • Removed /changelog, generate_changelog(), and hidden(); remove their calls and Cadwyn() changelog arguments, keeping the wrapped instructions. changelog_url=None and include_changelog_url_in_schema=False still work with a DeprecationWarning until 10.0. Generate your own changelog if needed; backports-strenum is no longer a dependency (#487).
  • Removed Cadwyn(openapi_prefix=...); configure your server's root path instead (#488).
  • Removed Cadwyn(api_version_header_name=...); use api_version_parameter_name instead.
  • Removed Cadwyn.add_header_versioned_routers(). Put the versions and their changes in a VersionBundle, then include the latest routers with generate_and_include_versioned_routers().
  • Removed Version.version_changes, HeadVersion.version_changes, and VersionBundle.version_dates; use changes and version_values, respectively.
  • .had(alias=...) and .didnt_have("alias") now update validation and serialization aliases derived from the old alias, so older versions use the documented key and reject data with only the old key. Add request and response migrations, or remove the alias change to keep the old key (required for HeadVersion); see alias migrations (#465).
  • Request and response migrations by schema now run for matching union members (Union[A, B], Optional[A]) and through Annotated and named aliases; whole-union migrations take precedence within a version change. Remove duplicate path migrations, return model instances for member response migrations, and migrate HTTP errors by path (migrate_http_errors=False for members). See union migrations for new error cases (#530).
  • Supported list[Model] and dict[str, Model] request bodies now preserve extras, set fields, and aliased values, and rerun factories for unset fields. Check code using extras, exclude_unset, or stateful factories, and set fields in a migration if older clients need them; changed models, dependency overrides, and other unsupported shapes keep their previous behavior (#566).
  • Computed fields no longer enter request.body or the latest model as input. Compute values in migrations that need them, and stop reading them from model_extra; responses and models that override model_dump() keep their previous behavior (#570).
  • Request bodies that FastAPI reads as bytes are no longer reparsed as JSON by Cadwyn, so migrations and body params may now receive bytes or defaults. Send Content-Type: application/json, or set strict_content_type=False on the app, router, or route (#531).
  • After restoring request validation aliases, Cadwyn reports the restored body's errors without rerunning the latest dependencies. Update handlers for CadwynHeadRequestValidationError and dependencies relying on that retry; delete rejected values in migrations if you need defaults supplied by custom core schemas (#563).
  • migrate_response_body() now restores validation aliases only for missing keys that would certainly make validation fail, as routes do. Set validation keys explicitly in other cases; restored responses now report their own errors, so update handlers and tests (#565).
  • Response fields with different validation and serialization aliases and defaults supplied only by custom core schemas now keep their values in migrate_response_body(). Invalid values now raise errors in routes too; delete them in response migrations or from latest_body to get the default (#565).
  • Renaming a field now fails at startup when a base or subclass would retain the old name alongside the new one. Rename it in the declaring base and, in the same version, in subclasses or other bases that retain it; to preserve both fields, add the old-version field with existed_as() instead. See inherited fields (#525, #581).
  • .didnt_exist now fails at startup if the schema would still inherit that field from a base. Delete it from the base in the same version too (#582).
  • Json[...] fields in supported bodies with unchanged schemas now preserve client strings, e.g. Json[Any] keeps "123" instead of giving 123. Encode client values once instead of twice; migrations that encode values still work, subject to known limitations (#538).
  • A param or dependency named body, or named after a body alias, no longer replaces the request body accidentally. For affected forms, files, and embedded bodies, make path migrations read the body or request.form; replace uploads in a migration, or read a replacement dependency's value explicitly (#526).
  • On FastAPI 0.158.2+, dependencies and overrides alongside an endpoint's form model now get their own form values, fixing defaults and 500 errors, including omitted optional models. Remove workarounds; conflicting shared values now raise CadwynError, so use distinct names or aliases, or read the form from Request instead of a whole-body param (see limitations) (#527).
  • On FastAPI 0.158.2+, when a request omits an optional form model and other params read the form, those params now get the untouched form values and the keys that a request migration sets, as in plain FastAPI; the model gets the migrated body only if it has fields of the model. A collection reaches them as repeated form values. Remove lost-value workarounds; a migrated body that isn't a dict, or that has a dict or a nested collection as a value, raises CadwynError (#529).
  • On FastAPI 0.158.2+, dependency form models retain unused AliasChoices keys as extras. Stop sending unused aliases when the model forbids extra fields, or allow extras if you need them (#527).
  • On FastAPI 0.153.0+, supported unions of form models preserve lists, sets, and tuples from validators or migrations instead of reducing them to one item. Accept the container or select its last item explicitly; conflicting field shapes keep the old behavior before FastAPI 0.161.0 and raise CadwynError on newer versions (#532).
  • Plain enums and flags with enum(...) instructions now reach endpoints as latest members; older enums accept matching latest members and flag combinations with no unknown bits. Compare union fields to members rather than raw values, use migrations if you relied on _missing_ replacing known members, and use isinstance(member, MyEnum) to distinguish latest members (#521).
  • Versioned enums now preserve aliases, nonmember(), @member, definition order, and custom attributes, and had() follows the class body. Send member values, treat @member functions as members, and update OpenAPI snapshots. Custom __new__ must recreate attributes from member values or copying fails; compute attributes from the value instead (see Enum migrations) (#555).
  • enum(MyEnum).had(member=auto()) now honors the enum's _generate_next_value_. Pass explicit values to preserve the old values (#554).
  • Container defaults and metadata preserve subclass types and attributes; unsafe copies raise SchemaGenerationError. Use plain containers for versioned classes or callables, and break cycles through factories (see Defaults) (#564).
  • had(...) now rejects the identical current object even when it is unequal to itself, such as a shared math.nan. Remove the redundant instruction (#541).
  • schema(M).validator(M.check_a).didnt_exist no longer removes another validator when check_a holds a function named like it, such as check_b in check_a = field_validator("a")(check_b). It now removes check_a, or raises CadwynStructureError if the function backs several validators; then pass the attribute name, e.g. schema(M).validator("check_a").didnt_exist (#133).

docs.text:
• FastAPI WebSocket routes now support endpoint("/ws", ["WEBSOCKET"]) with .existed, .didnt_exist, and .had(path=..., name=..., dependencies=...). HTTP methods cannot be mixed into a WebSocket selector; data converters remain HTTP-only. Refs #67.
  • Pass openapi_customizer to Cadwyn() to customize each generated OpenAPI document with its selected version, or None for the unversioned document. The synchronous callback returns the edited dict or a replacement dict (#255).
  • Remove a validator assigned as a model attribute, such as check_x = field_validator("x")(func), with schema(M).validator("check_x").didnt_exist (#133).
  • Version leaf models' Pydantic settings, including their generic parametrizations, with schema(Model).had(config=ConfigDict(...)); supported keys control extra fields, name and alias validation, whitespace stripping, freezing, titles, JSON schema extras, and arbitrary types. Unsupported keys and unchanged values are rejected, including in HeadVersion; rendering reports the model and key when a config callable's source, defaults, or bindings cannot be rendered safely (#91).
  • Pass run_background_tasks_of_latest_version_dependencies=True to Cadwyn() or generate_versioned_routers() to run tasks added during the latest dependency solve even when the endpoint has no BackgroundTasks param (#568).

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Documented that responses are validated twice: a model object that an endpoint returns runs its validators and model_post_init again (#592).
  • Type checkers now accept unions in convert_request_to_next_version_for() and convert_response_to_previous_version_for() (#530).
  • had(...) instructions now accept distinct values that compare equal, such as True and 1, instead of rejecting real changes. Unknown objects use identity; field errors say of "Model" instead of from "Model" (see instruction comparisons) (#541).

docs.title: Deprecated
docs.text: • Dropping latest-dependency tasks when the endpoint has no BackgroundTasks param now warns once per route; 10.0 will run them. Enable run_background_tasks_of_latest_version_dependencies=True now, and add each task only in the current_dependency_solver == "fastapi" run to avoid duplicates. See background tasks for warning limits (#568).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Fixed missing runtime annotation names in version changes, schema generation, and versioned-router generation, so typing.get_type_hints() can inspect them (#485).
  • Generated WebSocket routes now select the API version from headers, paths, or a constant default, including date fallback, and keep the version context through connection cleanup. Missing or invalid versions are rejected before acceptance; callable defaults require an explicit version for WebSockets, while unversioned sockets keep working with an empty preselected version. Refs #67.
  • Client disconnects no longer interrupt FastAPI's upload cleanup on Cadwyn's unversioned routes or when dependencies fail before the versioned endpoint wrapper runs, including with user BaseHTTPMiddleware layers (#594). Middleware dispatch, context visibility, exceptions, and responses keep their existing behavior; no app changes are needed. Standard disk closes run in daemon threads, so the cleanup deadline bounds the request wait and a permanently blocked close cannot prevent process exit.
  • Plain enums and flags with enum(...) instructions now work in supported lazy Iterable and Generator request fields without consuming items early (#591). Strict responses and opaque validation paths retain their previous behavior; see known limitations.
  • Enum copies now preserve extra attributes and slots assigned outside construction, including metaclass-assigned labels, on unchanged members. Constructor-produced state is rebuilt for each version (#589).
  • Responses whose validation aliases are restored now run model validators once, avoiding duplicated side effects in routes and migrate_response_body() (#565).
  • Supported request and response bodies with versioned plain enums or flags no longer fail with a 500; omitted enum defaults work on FastAPI before 0.148 when that version has the member. See known limitations for strict responses and unsupported containers (#521).
  • On FastAPI 0.153.0+, unions of form models no longer fail with a 500 for supported container fields; optional unions also receive their data on 0.161.0+ (#532).
  • Models with schema instructions no longer fail to copy annotations such as Final[int], TypeGuard, TypeIs, or ClassVar[Final[...]] (#576).
  • Background tasks can now read UploadFile params, including on disconnects and with generated routers outside Cadwyn. Uploads introduced by migrations are also closed, even if later replaced or removed; see upload cleanup for limits.
  • Versioned mixin enums now support vars() and __dict__, and enums declaring __slots__ no longer fail to copy (#555).
  • In supported request bodies with unchanged schemas, Json[...] fields accepting strings or string-enum members no longer fail with a 500 (#538).

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• The cadwyn command can import modules from the current directory again, so cadwyn render module data.schemas --app=main:app --version=... works when run from the folder that contains main.py and data/. Before, it failed with ModuleNotFoundError unless it was run as python -m cadwyn. Cadwyn 1.0.2 had fixed this, but later versions stopped putting the current directory on sys.path.
  • The how-to examples for changing schemas are now tested, which removed their unused imports and added the missing import of the version changes in the "Narrow the type" example.
  • Fixed documentation examples that failed or did the opposite of what they described: reversed field renames in the data migration and rename-a-field examples, the migrate_response_body() call without its versions argument, swapped "adding" and "removing" enum member examples, a VersionChangeWithSideEffects example without instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version, a hidden() example that changed path params (which Cadwyn rejects), a "remove a required field" recipe that left HEAD without the default it needs, and missing or wrong imports in several examples.
  • The examples on the "Version changes", "Changelogs", and "Enum migrations" documentation pages are now tested. This fixed the example of migrating HTTP errors, which changed 400 to 404 instead of changing the latest 404 back to 400, the example of returning an internal representation, which unpacked an object as a dict, and missing imports in the current_dependency_solver example. The "Version changes" page also no longer suggests renaming an inherited field in each child schema instead of the parent, which keeps the old field next to the new one. The "Enum migrations" examples now show the enum they change (class MyEnum(str, Enum)).
  • The code examples on the "Schema migrations", "API version parameter", "Schema generation", "Endpoint migrations", and "Main App" pages are now tested. Examples that could not run now work as written: they no longer import from hypothetical versions and my_versions modules or pass ... to Cadwyn(), and the validator examples no longer have unused imports. The "Schema migrations" page now says to rename an inherited field in the schema that declares it, because renaming it in a subclass keeps the old field next to the new one. The cadwyn render examples on the "Schema generation" page now say to run them from the app's directory.
  • Fixed documentation claims that contradicted Cadwyn's behavior: that Cadwyn only supports date-based versions, that api_version_parameter_name defaults to "X-API-VERSION", that a schema can have both default and default_factory, that validators can reject values with TypeError, and references to the data.vXXXX_XX_XX packages that Cadwyn no longer generates.
  • With FastAPI 0.158.2 or newer, endpoints with an optional form model (e.g. body: Annotated[Optional[MyModel], Form()] = None) no longer fail with a 500 error in every API version when the request has none of the model's form fields. Request migrations get None as the body, and the endpoint gets the param's default (#495).
  • With FastAPI 0.158.2, endpoints that take a form model no longer fail with a 500 error, and endpoints that take an optional form model now get its form data instead of None. Cadwyn handled the way FastAPI looks up form models only from FastAPI 0.159.0, while FastAPI changed it in 0.158.2 (#495).
  • With FastAPI 0.158.2 or newer, a form field or an embedded body param (Body(embed=True)) of a dependency override that has the same name as the endpoint's form model param (e.g. body: Annotated[MyModel, Form()] in the endpoint and body: str = Form() in the override) now gets its own value from the form model's data instead of the whole form model, like in FastAPI itself. If the data has no value for it, it gets its default. Before, this failed with a 500 error, or, if the param accepted the form model's data (e.g. body: Any = Form()), gave it the whole form model. Requests in which another param of an override takes the whole body, a required param has no value in the data, or the form has a value for a param that the form model of the request's API version doesn't have a field for (e.g. a field that only newer versions of the model have, or, for a union of form models, a field that only the members that the request doesn't match have), work as before (#496).
  • With FastAPI 0.161.0 or newer, endpoints that take a union of form models (e.g. body: Annotated[Union[ModelA, ModelB], Form()]) no longer fail with a 500 error in every API version, including when the models have set, frozenset, or tuple fields. Endpoints that take an optional union of form models (e.g. body: Annotated[Optional[Union[ModelA, ModelB]], Form()] = None) now get the form data instead of None, and no longer fail with a 500 error when the request has none of the models' form fields. Request migrations of these endpoints get the form data of the model that the request matches as the body, or None if the request has no form data for the optional union. Requests whose body has a list, set, or tuple in a field that a model of the union takes a single value for (e.g. a field of type Any that a validator or a migration fills with a list, or a field that a model which allows extra fields doesn't have) behave as before, because FastAPI would give the field only one of the values.
  • On Python 3.11 and newer, enum(...) instructions on a Flag or IntFlag enum no longer make every route and the OpenAPI return a 500 error. The enum of each version has the members of that version, combines them like a hand-written enum, and keeps the enum's boundary (#522).
  • Request bodies, responses, and fields typed by a native type alias that refers to itself (Python 3.12+), directly or through other type aliases, no longer fail with a 500 error in every API version when the alias only contains builtin types, such as type JSON = dict[str, JSON] | list[JSON] | str | int | None, and other such aliases. Recursive type aliases that contain anything else, such as models, enums, other classes, forward refs, or Annotated, still can't be versioned: instead of a RecursionError, the first request now fails with a SchemaGenerationError that names the alias (#524).
  • With FastAPI 0.158.2 or newer, when a request has none of the fields of an optional form model param without an alias (e.g. body: Annotated[Optional[MyModel], Form()] = None), or, with FastAPI 0.161.0 or newer, of an optional union of form models, a dict that a request migration sets as the body (e.g. request.body = {"name": "x"}) now reaches the endpoint, the dependencies that declare the same form model under the same param name, and the dependency overrides that declare the same form model. Before, they got None, or a 500 error for some unions. A body that the form model rejects now fails with a 500 error, as it does when the form supplies the model. Everything else behaves as before, including a dict with none of the form model's fields (e.g. {}), which gives the param its default, as FastAPI does for a form, a body that isn't a dict or that has a key named like the param (e.g. {"body": {"name": "x"}}), another form model or form field with the same name as the param, a param that gets the whole body (e.g. payload: dict = Body() in an override of a dependency that only the latest version has), a form field that isn't a form model (e.g. x: str = Form("d") in an override), a dependency that declares a form model under another param name, a key that another param reads next to a form model that allows or forbids extra fields, and, for a union, a body with values that FastAPI would change when it validates them as form data (e.g. an empty string, or a one-item list in an extra field) (#529).
  • Request bodies with Json[...] fields (e.g. data: Json[dict]), including form models and nested models, no longer fail with a 500 error in the latest API version and in the older versions whose body models are the same as the latest version's. Request migrations still get the parsed values of these fields. If Cadwyn can't be sure that the latest version gets what the client has sent everywhere in the body, the request behaves as before. Known limitations lists these cases (#523).

This release fixes many long-standing bugs, most of them reported by users. Most apps can upgrade without changes. It is a major release because some fixes change wrong behavior that apps or their clients may rely on. Before upgrading, check the Breaking entries and the Upgrade note below. In short:

  • Cadwyn now requires Pydantic 2.11.5 or newer.
  • Older API versions use their own versions of the models inside generic models such as Page[Item].
  • Older API versions of endpoints with postponed annotations validate request bodies with their own models.
  • schema(Child).field(...) instructions for inherited fields no longer leak into parent and sibling models.
  • Annotated[T, Depends(f)] dependencies use the versions of models and enums that the request's API version has, in the versions that change them.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• schema(Model).had(description=...) gives older versions of a model their own OpenAPI description (#168).
  • Documented how to serve endpoints to requests without an API version, e.g. the OAuth2 token endpoint (#230).
  • Documented how to use fastapi-pagination with Cadwyn (#191).
  • Documented that request and response migrations only run for the schema that the route uses directly, not for that schema nested in other schemas.
  • Documented that computed fields that return versioned models keep the latest versions of these models in older API versions.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Breaking: Cadwyn now requires Pydantic 2.11.5 or newer.
  • Breaking: generic models such as Page[Item] now use the versioned copies of their type args in requests, responses, and OpenAPI (#416, #420). Older versions validate and serialize these args with their own models, so older clients that relied on the latest models inside generics may need converters for the generics: converters for Item don't run for the items of Page[Item]. The OpenAPI names of some generics change, and migrate_response_body no longer accepts instances of the latest models inside them. See Generic models for details.
  • Breaking: schema(Child).field(...).had(...) and .didnt_have(...) for an inherited field now change it only in Child and its subclasses, not in its parent and siblings (#466). To keep the old behavior, give the instruction to the parent instead. If a parent renames such a field, the subclass's changes follow the new name only through single, non-generic inheritance. cadwyn render now renders each model's own attributes in each version. See Fields that a schema inherits for diamonds and generics.
  • Breaking: dependencies declared as Annotated[T, Depends(f)], Annotated[T, Security(f)], or Annotated[f, Depends()] now use the version's own copy of f in the versions that change the models or enums its parameters validate (#467). Requests that relied on the latest dependency can now get a 422, and in these versions the dependency receives the version's copies of models and enums, so compare them by value rather than with isinstance or is. See Versioned dependencies.
  • Self-referencing models that don't have, refer to, or pass on any instructions are no longer copied for every version: generate_versioned_models(versions)[version][Category] is Category.
  • app.dependency_overrides is now FastAPI's plain attribute. Removed the undocumented cadwyn.applications.FakeDependencyOverridesProvider and the Cadwyn.dependency_overrides property.
  • Type checkers now accept assigning an APIRouter to app.router, as in FastAPI. Cadwyn still needs its own router there, so don't replace it.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Upgrade note: older API versions of endpoints with postponed (from __future__ import annotations) or quoted request body annotations used the latest models since 6.0.1. Now they use their own models, as documented, so clients that kept sending the latest shape may get a 422.
  • Fixed apps failing to start, or every request failing with a 500 (RecursionError), when models refer to themselves, e.g. children: "list[Category]" (#419). Where Cadwyn can't copy such models, it now raises a SchemaGenerationError that names them. See Models that refer to each other.
  • Fixed responses failing with a 500, and request bodies failing in non-head versions, when a required field validates a different key than it serializes to, e.g. validation_alias or serialization_alias (#260, #370). Bodies that worked before are unchanged.
  • Fixed OpenAPI documenting the API version header as optional when api_version_default_value isn't set (#277).
  • Fixed older API versions adding "example": {} to the OpenAPI of parameters declared with defaults such as = Query() (#417).
  • Fixed Cadwyn() failing on FastAPI 0.145.0 and newer (#462).
  • Fixed requests without a body failing with a 500 on FastAPI 0.151.0 and newer when the endpoint or its dependencies have embedded optional body params, a None default that their type rejects, or a quoted body annotation.
  • Fixed apps served with uvicorn module:app returning a 500 for every request since 7.1.1.
  • Fixed Cadwyn(strict_content_type=False) having no effect.
  • Fixed uploaded files declared as bytes, in endpoints and dependencies, arriving empty in non-head versions. These versions now hold such uploads in memory twice per request. Dependencies that move an upload only when current_dependency_solver is "fastapi" may now see it moved back to its start; see Dependency re-execution warning.
  • Fixed embedded request bodies failing in non-head versions when the endpoint has a parameter named body or a body alias that matches another parameter's name.
  • Fixed enums without enum instructions being copied for every version, which broke strict models.
  • Fixed versioned dependencies:
    • functools.partial dependencies lost their annotations;
    • dependencies described only by __signature__ lost their parameter types;
    • async generator dependencies didn't receive exceptions raised after yield;
    • Depends(scope=...) was lost;
    • app.dependency_overrides was ignored in older API versions for class instances, bound methods, and partials;
    • parameter defaults such as = Query() were shared between versions and apps.
  • Fixed startup failures for:
    • functools.lru_cache dependencies with postponed annotations;
    • dependency annotations that use names imported under TYPE_CHECKING on Python 3.14;
    • dependency return annotations that only type checkers can evaluate (Cadwyn no longer versions them, like FastAPI).
  • Fixed older API versions failing on models that use:
    • typing.Self;
    • annotations that can't be rebuilt, such as a bare Callable or Unpack[Ts];
    • default factories without a signature;
    • names imported under TYPE_CHECKING on Python 3.14;
    • generic fields that parametrize generics with their own type parameters, e.g. items: list[Wrapper[T]].
  • Fixed TypeError: unhashable type in older API versions for unhashable request body or response model annotations.
  • Fixed schema(...).field(...).didnt_have(...) having no effect on title, description, examples, and deprecated declared through Annotated[..., Field(...)].
  • Fixed didnt_have("title"), didnt_have("min_length"), and didnt_have(...) failing with TypeError on Annotated types with validators, Len, Strict, or AllowInfNan.
  • Fixed had(default=...) and had(default_factory=...) failing with pydantic's TypeError at startup when they leave a field with both a default and a default factory. Cadwyn now raises InvalidGenerationInstructionError, and the instruction's value replaces the one from Annotated[..., Field(...)].
  • Fixed the deprecated /changelog failing with a 500 for self-referencing models, and on every call after the first one for instructions on inherited fields.
  • Fixed type checking with Pydantic 2.14 and ty 0.0.86.

docs.title: Setting up the environment
docs.text:
• The minimum supported version is Python 3.11. It is recommended to manage multiple Python versions on your system with uv
  • Running the full local check suite also requires Node.js and npm for link validation

  • Run make to see the available developer commands

  • Install uv

  • Run make install to install the project and standalone developer tools
  • Run make hooks to install the prek git hooks
  • Run make check to verify that the local CI-equivalent checks pass

make install uses uv to create the project environment with every development and optional dependency. It also installs prek and tox with the tox-uv plugin as standalone tools so repeated checks start quickly.

Skip make hooks if you already manage hooks with Git's core.hooksPath setting. You can still run every hook manually with make lint.

docs.text:
1. Fork the Cadwyn repository
  2. Clone your fork locally with git
  3. Set up the environment

  5. Commit your changes to git

  7. Open a pull request. Give the pull request a descriptive title indicating what was changed

docs.title: Guidelines for writing code
docs.text:
• Before changing Cadwyn's behavior, read Design decisions and trade-offs. It lists what Cadwyn has already accepted, what it deliberately doesn't do, and when a change counts as breaking
  • To find your way around the code, read Architecture. It describes how Cadwyn generates the models and routes of every version and what happens during a request
  • Code should be Pythonic and zen
  • All code should be fully typed. This is enforced via ruff and ty
  • When complex types are required, use type aliases
  • If something cannot be typed correctly due to the limitations of the type checkers, use typing.cast to resolve the issue. However, use typing.cast only as a last resort, after exhausting all other options of type narrowing, such as isinstance() checks and type guards
  • Use ty: ignore once you have verified that the line is correct, but ty has issues with it
  • If you are adding or modifying existing code, make sure that it's fully tested. 100% test coverage is mandatory, and will be checked on the PR using Github Actions
  • When adding a new public interface, make sure you have included it in the concept documentation located in docs/concepts/. If applicable, add or modify examples in the docs related to the new functionality

docs.title: Writing and running tests
docs.text:
Tests are contained within the tests directory, and follow roughly the same directory structure as the cadwyn module. Place each test according to the public interface it exercises. If a test has no natural location in that structure, check whether it is testing an internal implementation detail that would be better covered through a public interface.

Keep tests atomic. Separate distinct positive and negative scenarios, and use parametrization when the same behavior needs to be checked with several inputs.

make check runs the local CI-equivalent suite with tox's default automatic parallelism. It runs the supported Python test matrix, tutorial tests, coverage, prek linting, documentation build, link validation, and package build checks. Each supported Python test environment runs ty before its tests.

If prek, tox, or the tox-uv plugin is missing, the Makefile will stop early and print the matching uv tool install ... command to install it.

Use make lint to run only the prek hooks. For a focused test run, use uv run pytest followed by the test path and any pytest options.

Name tests using the what, when, expected convention:

test__{what}__{when}__{expected}

what is the function or public interface under test, when describes the conditions in which it is exercised, and expected states the observable result. Prefer concrete outcomes such as should_return_404 or should_raise_router_generation_error over generic suffixes such as error, ok, or numbered variants. A test name should let a reader understand a failure without first opening its implementation.

docs.title: Running type checkers
docs.text:
We use ty to enforce type safety. It runs before the test suite on every supported Python version. You can run it against your active project environment with:

uv run ty check

docs.title: How to...
docs.text:
This section serves as a guide to help you create new versions effectively and maintain your old versions with ease. It consists of a collection of scenarios for different types of breaking changes.

To follow this guide, choose a type of an entity that you'd like to alter (an endpoint, a schema, etc), find the respective article, and follow its instructions. Repeat for every breaking change you would like to do.

Versioning is a complex topic with more pitfalls than you'd expect so please: do not try to skip this guide. Otherwise, your code will quickly get unmaintainable. Please also note that any of these scenarios can be combined in any way even within a single version change, though it's recommended to keep the version changes atomic as described in methodology section.

docs.title: Version with paths and numbers instead of headers and dates
docs.text:
Cadwyn uses version headers with ISO dates by default for versioning. However, you can use any strings instead of ISO dates and/or you can use path version prefixes instead of version headers. Here's our quickstart tutorial example but using version numbers and path prefixes:

Feel free to mix and match the API version formats and version locations as you see fit. But beware that Cadwyn does not support version waterfalling for arbitrary strings as versions.

import uuid

from cadwyn import VersionedAPIRouter
from cadwyn.applications import Cadwyn
from cadwyn.structure import (
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    Version,
    VersionBundle,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    endpoint,
    schema,
)
from cadwyn.structure.versions import HeadVersion
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class BaseUser(BaseModel):
    pass


class UserCreateRequest(BaseUser):
    default_address: str
    addresses_to_create: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)


class UserResource(BaseUser):
    id: uuid.UUID


class UserAddressResource(BaseModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    value: str


class UserAddressResourceList(BaseModel):
    data: list[UserAddressResource]


class ReplaceUserAddressWithListOfAddresses(VersionChange):
    """Users can now store multiple addresses instead of a single address so they can choose among delivery locations."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser).field("addresses").didnt_exist,
        schema(BaseUser).field("address").existed_as(type=str, info=Field()),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(UserCreateRequest)
    def change_address_to_multiple_items(request: RequestInfo) -> None:
        request.body["addresses"] = [request.body.pop("address")]

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(UserResource)
    def change_addresses_to_single_item(response: ResponseInfo) -> None:
        # Need to assert addresses length somewhere in business logic
        response.body["address"] = response.body["addresses"][0]


class MoveUserAddressesToSubresource(VersionChange):
    """User addresses are now separate resources with stable IDs, allowing clients to retrieve each address independently."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser)
        .field("addresses")
        .existed_as(type=list[str], info=Field()),
        schema(UserCreateRequest).field("default_address").didnt_exist,
        endpoint(
            "/{api_version}/users/{user_id}/addresses", ["GET"]
        ).didnt_exist,
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(UserCreateRequest)
    def change_addresses_to_default_address(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["default_address"] = request.body["addresses"].pop(0)
        # Save data to still be able to keep the old behavior of creating addresses
        request.body["addresses_to_create"] = request.body.pop("addresses")

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(UserResource)
    def change_addresses_to_list(response: ResponseInfo) -> None:
        response.body["addresses"] = [
            id["value"] for id in response.body["_prefetched_addresses"]
        ]


class RemoveAddressesToCreateFromLatestUserSchema(VersionChange):
    """Stop accepting 'addresses_to_create' when creating users.

    Additional addresses are now managed as separate resources.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest).field("addresses_to_create").didnt_exist,
    )


version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(RemoveAddressesToCreateFromLatestUserSchema),
    Version("v10", MoveUserAddressesToSubresource),
    Version("v9", ReplaceUserAddressWithListOfAddresses),
    Version("v8"),
)


router = VersionedAPIRouter(tags=["Users"])
database_parody = {}


@router.post("/{api_version}/users", response_model=UserResource)
async def create_user(user: UserCreateRequest):
    id_ = uuid.uuid4()
    database_parody[id_] = {"id": id_}
    addresses = create_user_addresses(
        id_, [user.default_address, *user.addresses_to_create]
    )
    return database_parody[id_] | {"_prefetched_addresses": addresses}


@router.get("/{api_version}/users/{user_id}", response_model=UserResource)
async def get_user(user_id: uuid.UUID):
    return {
        "id": user_id,
        "_prefetched_addresses": (await get_user_addresses(user_id))["data"],
    }


def create_user_addresses(user_id: uuid.UUID, addresses: list[str]):
    database_parody[f"addr_{user_id}"] = [
        {"id": uuid.uuid4(), "value": address} for address in addresses
    ]
    return database_parody[f"addr_{user_id}"]


@router.get(
    "/{api_version}/users/{user_id}/addresses",
    response_model=UserAddressResourceList,
)
async def get_user_addresses(user_id: uuid.UUID):
    return {"data": database_parody[f"addr_{user_id}"]}


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=version_bundle,
    api_version_parameter_name="api_version",
    api_version_format="string",
    api_version_location="path",
)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

docs.title: Change the business logic in a new version
docs.text:
First, ask yourself: are you sure a behavioral change is really necessary? Are you sure it is not possible to keep the same logic for both versions?
