Or at least make the behavior depend on the received data? Behavioral changes (or side effects) are the least maintainable part of almost any versioning approach. They produce the largest footprint on your code. So if you are not careful, your logic will be littered with version checks.

But if you are certain that you need to make a breaking behavioral change, Cadwyn has all the tools to minimize its impact as much as possible.

docs.title: Calling endpoint causes unexpected data modifications
docs.text: Use an if statement with a side effect.

docs.title: Calling endpoint doesn't cause expected data modifications
docs.text: Use an if statement with a side effect.

docs.title: Calling endpoint doesn't cause expected additional actions (e.g. Webhooks)
docs.text: Use an if statement with a side effect.

docs.title: Change the status code or a message in an HTTP error
docs.text: You can migrate anything about the error in a version change.

docs.title: Introduce a new error or remove an old error
docs.text: Use an if statement with a side effect.

docs.title: Change endpoints in a new version
Add a new endpoint
docs.text: It is not a breaking change so it's recommended to add it to all versions. If you believe that you still need it, use following migration.

docs.title: Delete an old endpoint
docs.text: See concepts

docs.title: Change an attribute of an endpoint
docs.text:
Modifying a "decorative" attribute such as a description or a summary is not a breaking change so apply it to all versions.

However, you are still free to change almost any attribute of an endpoint in an old version. See concepts docs.

docs.title: Rename an endpoint
docs.text: Renaming endpoints is the same as changing their "path" attribute. See concepts docs for more details.

docs.title: Add a field to OpenAPI schemas
To response schema
docs.text:
Let's say that we decided to expose the creation date of user's account with a created_at field in our API. This is not a breaking change so a new version is completely unnecessary. However, if you believe that you absolutely have to make a new version, then you can simply follow the recommended approach below but add a version change with field didn't exist instruction.

You just need to add created_at field into users.UserResource.

Now you have everything you need at your disposal: field created_at is available in all versions and your users do not even need to do any extra actions. Just make sure that the data for it is available in all versions too. If it's not: make the field optional.

docs.title: To both request and response schemas
Field is optional
docs.text:
Let's say we want our users to be able to specify a middle name but it is nullable. It is not a breaking change so no new version is necessary whether it is requests or responses.

You just need to add an optional middle_name: str | None = None field into users.BaseUser as if you were working with a barebones FastAPI app.

docs.title: With compatible default value in older versions
docs.text:
Let's say that our users had a field country that defaulted to USA but our product is now used well beyond United States so we want to make this field required in the HEAD version.

  1. Remove default="USA" from users.UserCreateRequest

  2. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01:

    from cadwyn import (
    RequestInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    schema,
)
from users import UserCreateRequest


class MakeUserCountryRequired(VersionChange):
    """'country' is now required when creating a user because the API
    serves users outside the United States and can no longer assume 'USA'.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest).field("country").had(default="USA"),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(UserCreateRequest)
    def add_default_value_to_country_field_in_request(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["country"] = request.body.get("country", "USA")

  3. Add this migration into the version bundle:

    from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2001_01_01 import MakeUserCountryRequired

version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(),
    Version("2001-01-01", MakeUserCountryRequired),
    Version("2000-01-01"),
)

That's it. Our old schemas will now contain a default but in HEAD country will be required. You might notice a weirdness: if we set a default in the old version, why would we also write a migration? That's because of a sad implementation detail of pydantic that prevents us from using defaults from old versions.

docs.title: With incompatible default value in older versions
docs.text:
Let's say that we want to add a required field phone to our users. However, older versions did not have such a field at all. This means that the field is going to be nullable (or nonexistent) in the old versions but required in the HEAD version. This also means that older versions contain a wider type (str | None) than the HEAD version (str). So when we try to migrate request bodies from the older versions to HEAD -- we might receive a ValidationError because None is not an acceptable value for phone field in the new version. Whenever we have a problem like this, when older version contains more data or a wider type set of data, we can simply define a wider type in our HEAD version and then narrow it in latest.

So we will make phone nullable in HEAD, then make it required in latest, and then make it nullable again in older versions, thus making it possible to convert all of our requests to HEAD.

  1. Add phone field of type str | None with a default=None to users.BaseUser
  2. Add phone field of type str | None with a default=None to users.UserResource because all users created with older versions of our API won't have phone numbers.

  3. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01 which will make sure that phone is not nullable in 2001_01_01:

    from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from users import UserCreateRequest


class MakeUserPhoneNonNullableInLatest(VersionChange):
    """New user requests now require a phone number so accounts can support
    SMS verification and two-factor authentication.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest).field("phone").had(type=str),
        schema(UserCreateRequest).field("phone").didnt_have("default"),
    )

  4. Add the following version change to versions.v2001_01_01 (right under the version change above) which will make sure that phone is nullable in 2000_01_01:

    class AddRequiredPhoneToUser(VersionChange):
    """New user requests now require a phone number so accounts can support
    SMS verification and two-factor authentication.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest)
        .field("phone")
        .had(type=str | None, default=None),
    )

  5. Add both migrations into our VersionBundle:

    from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2001_01_01 import (
    AddRequiredPhoneToUser,
    MakeUserPhoneNonNullableInLatest,
)

version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(MakeUserPhoneNonNullableInLatest),
    Version("2001-01-01", AddRequiredPhoneToUser),
    Version("2000-01-01"),
)

See how we didn't remove the phone field from old versions? Instead, we allowed a nullable phone field to be passed into both old UserResource and old UserCreateRequest. This gives our users new functionality without needing to update their API version. It is one of the best parts of Cadwyn's approach: our users can get years worth of updates without switching their API version and without their integration getting broken.

docs.title: Change the type incompatibly
docs.text: If your data had a type int and you want to change it to a str in a new version, then your data from the new version can easily break the responses of the old versions, thus making it data versioning, not API versioning -- as you are versioning the fundamental structures the user is operating on instead of just the API.

docs.title: Expand the type
docs.text:
Suppose your clients could choose a role for your users. Originally, it was only possible to choose admin or regular but you would like to expand it to moderator which has all the permissions of an admin except assigning other admins.

This is not a breaking change in terms of requests but it can be a breaking change in terms of responses. So if you do consider it a breaking change in terms of responses, do the following:

  1. Add moderator value into users.UserRoleEnum

  2. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01:

    from cadwyn import (
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    enum,
)
from users import UserResource, UserRoleEnum


class AddModeratorRoleToUser(VersionChange):
    """Users can now have a 'moderator' role with administrative access but
    without permission to create or remove admins, enabling safer delegation.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        enum(UserRoleEnum).didnt_have("moderator"),
    )

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(UserResource)
    def change_moderator_to_regular(response: ResponseInfo):
        if response.body["role"] == "moderator":
            response.body["role"] = "regular"

You convert moderators to regulars in older versions because it is a safer choice for your users.

docs.title: Why enum expansion is a breaking change for responses
docs.text:
Suppose your schema contained a list that contains euros and/or dollars. To unmarshal the JSON, your client takes the JSON string and tries to convert it to a list of euros and/or dollars. If there appears Georgian lari in the list, the client will fail to unmarshal such a list, which makes adding an enum value a breaking change for a list of items.

If an API client expects Array<Euro | Dollar>, then Array<Euro> and Array<Dollar> would both be considered compatible responses but Array<Euro | Dollar | Lari> would not. That happens because Array<Euro | Dollar | Lari> is not a subtype of Array<Euro | Dollar> while Array<Euro> is.

In a sense, extending an enum that has USD with USD | EUR is equivalent to turning an int field into an int | str field, which is a breaking change. Hence extending an enum is often a breaking change and thus you might not need to solve this problem at all.

Additional resources:

  • https://github.com/OAI/OpenAPI-Specification/issues/1552
  • https://users.rust-lang.org/t/solved-is-adding-an-enum-variant-a-breaking-change/26721/5
  • https://github.com/graphql/graphql-js/issues/968

In these sections, we'll be working with Cadwyn's user response model: users.UserResource. Note that the main question here is "Will I be able to serialize this change to any of my versions?" as any change to responses can make them incompatible with the data in your database.

docs.title: Narrow the type
docs.text:
Suppose that previously users could specify their date of birth as a datetime instead of a date. You are planning to change that. You can solve this by making it a datetime in HEAD version, converting it to date in latest version, and then making it a datetime again in the old versions. So whenever you receive a request in an old version, it will get converted to HEAD version where it is a datetime. And whenever you receive a request in latest version, it will also be converted to HEAD where date will simply be casted to datetime with time = 00:00:00.

  1. Continue storing date_of_birth as a datetime in your database to avoid breaking any old behavior

  2. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01 which will turn date_of_birth into a date in 2001_01_01. Note how the validator is used to make sure that date_of_birth is converted to date in the latest version. It is only necessary in Pydantic 2 because it has no implicit casting from datetime to date.

    import datetime

from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import field_validator
from users import BaseUser


@field_validator("date_of_birth", mode="before")
def convert_date_of_birth_to_date(cls, v: datetime.date | datetime.datetime):
    if isinstance(v, datetime.datetime):
        return v.date()
    return v


class ChangeUserDateOfBirthFromDatetimeToDateInLatest(VersionChange):
    """'User.date_of_birth' is now a calendar date instead of a timestamp
    because a time of day is not meaningful for a birth date.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser).field("date_of_birth").had(type=datetime.date),
        # This step is only necessary in Pydantic 2 because datetime
        # won't be converted to date automatically.
        schema(BaseUser).validator(convert_date_of_birth_to_date).existed,
    )

  3. Add the following version change to versions.v2001_01_01 (right under the version change above) which will make sure that date_of_birth is a datetime in 2000_01_01:

    class ChangeUserDateOfBirthFromDatetimeToDate(VersionChange):
    """'User.date_of_birth' is now a calendar date instead of a timestamp
    because a time of day is not meaningful for a birth date.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser).field("date_of_birth").had(type=datetime.datetime),
        schema(BaseUser).validator(convert_date_of_birth_to_date).didnt_exist,
    )

  4. Add both migrations into the VersionBundle:

    from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2001_01_01 import (
    ChangeUserDateOfBirthFromDatetimeToDate,
    ChangeUserDateOfBirthFromDatetimeToDateInLatest,
)

version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(ChangeUserDateOfBirthFromDatetimeToDateInLatest),
    Version("2001-01-01", ChangeUserDateOfBirthFromDatetimeToDate),
    Version("2000-01-01"),
)

The process above is a bit complex, so let us break it down:

  1. date_of_birth field is a datetime in HEAD, a date in 2001, and a datetime again in 2000.
  2. You need a way to keep the 2000 behavior making it unavailable for users in 2001. Cadwyn always converts all requests to the HEAD version so:
    • When user creation requests are received from 2001, they are converted directly to HEAD, and pydantic casts date to datetime without any issue
    • When user get requests are received from 2001, they are converted directly from HEAD to latest, and the validator casts datetime to date (note that pydantic 1 would be able to do it even without a validator)
    • When user creation requests are received from 2000, they are converted directly to HEAD. They have the same type for date_of_birth, so Cadwyn easily processes them
    • When user get requests are received from 2000, they are converted directly from HEAD to 2000. They have the same type for date_of_birth, so Cadwyn easily processes them

All of these interactions are done internally by Cadwyn. As you see, the process is more than straightforward: requests are converted to HEAD, and responses are converted from HEAD.

Thus, you have kept the old behavior, added new constrained behavior, and minimized the impact on your business logic as business logic simply doesn't know that date_of_birth in requests is ever a date and that date_of_birth in responses is ever a date. All of this information is hidden in your migration.

Please note that unlike schemas, routes, and business logic, the migrations written above will likely never need to change because they describe the fundamental differences between the API versions, and these differences cannot be changed in the future because that would defeat the purpose of API versioning. This makes migrations effectively immutable and consequently very cheap to support.

docs.title: Change a schema that is not used in any endpoint
docs.text:
In some situations, you may want to use versioning not only for your OpenAPI schemas and endpoints but also within your code, for example to send versioned webhooks to your clients.

Suppose you want to change the type of an id field from integer to string:

from cadwyn import (
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel


# User from latest version
class User(BaseModel):
    id: str


class ChangeUserIdFromIntegerToString(VersionChange):
    """'User.id' is now a string so the API can support identifiers that are not numeric."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = [
        schema(User).field("id").had(type=int),
    ]

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(User)
    def change_id_to_int(response: ResponseInfo): ...

Unless there is an endpoint that has User as its response_model, this code will end up causing an error when you run the Cadwyn app. This is because Cadwyn tries to make sure that all of your converters apply to at least one endpoint. Otherwise, it would be too easy for you to make a mistake when writing converters for the wrong schemas.

To avoid it, set check_usage=False:

from cadwyn import (
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel


# User from latest version
class User(BaseModel):
    id: str


class ChangeUserIdFromIntegerToString(VersionChange):
    """'User.id' is now a string so the API can support identifiers that are not numeric."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = [
        schema(User).field("id").had(type=int),
    ]

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(User, check_usage=False)
    def change_id_to_int(response: ResponseInfo): ...

docs.title: Change field constraints or validators in OpenAPI schemas
Add or narrow constraints
docs.text:
Suppose you previously allowed users to have a name of arbitrary length but now you want to limit it to 250 characters because you are worried that some users may use inadequate lengths. You can't do this easily: if you simply add a max_length constraint to User.name, the existing data in your database might become incompatible with this field in UserResource. So as long as incompatible data is there or can get there from some version, you cannot add such a constraint to your responses. However, you can add it to your requests to prevent the creation of new user accounts with long names.

  1. Change max_length of users.UserCreateRequest.name to 250 in version 2001-01-01 by adding the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01. We do this instead of just adding the constraint to HEAD to make sure that old requests will get converted to HEAD successfully -- without facing the constraint:

    from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from users import UserCreateRequest


class LimitUserNamesTo250CharactersInLatest(VersionChange):
    """User names in creation requests are now limited to 250 characters
    to prevent impractically large values.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest).field("name").had(max_length=250),
    )

  2. Then add the following migration under the migration above in the same file:

    class LimitUserNamesTo250Characters(VersionChange):
    """User names in creation requests are now limited to 250 characters
    to prevent impractically large values.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest).field("name").didnt_have("max_length"),
    )

  3. Add both of these migrations to the version bundle:

    from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2001_01_01 import (
    LimitUserNamesTo250Characters,
    LimitUserNamesTo250CharactersInLatest,
)

version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(LimitUserNamesTo250CharactersInLatest),
    Version("2001-01-01", LimitUserNamesTo250Characters),
    Version("2000-01-01"),
)

So the HEAD version does not have this constraint, the latest does, and earlier versions do not.

  • Requests from 2000 will be converted directly to HEAD and will not face this constraint because HEAD does not have it
  • Requests from 2001 will first be validated by 2001 schemas with this constraint, and then will be converted to HEAD too

Note, however, that anyone using the old API versions will still be able to use arbitrary length names. If you want to prevent that, do the following:

  1. Check whether any users have names longer than 250 characters. If there are few or no users with such long names, then it may make sense to skip step 1. The other steps, however, cannot be skipped if you want to guarantee that your API gives no 500s at any point in the process
  2. Issue a 3-6 month warning to all users stating that you will make a breaking change affecting older versions. Mention that you will truncate old names that are longer than 250 characters and that users will no longer be able to create such long names even in old API versions
  3. After the deadline, add a max_length constraint to users.UserCreateRequest.name and remove the instructions of LimitUserNamesTo250CharactersInLatest and LimitUserNamesTo250Characters
  4. Release it to production
  5. Truncate all names that are too long in the database (preferably using a migration and a separate release)
  6. Remove the max_length constraint from users.UserCreateRequest.name
  7. Add the max_length constraint to users.BaseUser.name

This process seems quite complex but it's not Cadwyn-specific: if you want to safely and nicely version for your users, you will have to follow such a process even if you don't use any versioning framework at all.

docs.title: Remove or expand constraints
docs.text:
Suppose you previously allowed users to have a name length up to 50 characters but now you want to allow up to 250. It does not make sense to add this to a new API version. As it is not a breaking change, add it to all API versions by changing max_length of users.BaseUser.name to 250.

However, sometimes it can be considered a breaking change if a large portion of your users use your system to verify their data and rely on your system to return status code 422 if this field is invalid. In this case use the same approach as in constraint addition but use schema(UserCreateRequest).field("name").had(max_length=50) instead.

docs.title: Add or remove validators
docs.text: The approach above can be used to add or remove Pydantic validator functions using validator generation. Note that adding validators is the same as narrowing or adding constraints, which means that the same trick as above should be used.

docs.title: Remove a field from OpenAPI schemas
From response
docs.text:
Let's say that our API has a mandatory UserResource.date_of_birth field. Let's also say that our API has previously exposed user's zodiac sign. Our analysts have decided that it does not make sense to store or send this information as it does not affect the functionality and can be inferred from date of birth.

  1. Remove zodiac_sign field from users.UserResource

  2. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01:

    from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import Field
from users import UserResource


class RemoveZodiacSignFromUser(VersionChange):
    """User responses no longer include 'zodiac_sign' because it can be
    derived from 'date_of_birth' and is rarely used.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserResource)
        .field("zodiac_sign")
        .existed_as(type=str, info=Field(description="User's magical sign")),
    )

  3. Add this migration into the version bundle:

    # versions/__init__.py

from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2001_01_01 import RemoveZodiacSignFromUser

version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(),
    Version("2001-01-01", RemoveZodiacSignFromUser),
    Version("2000-01-01"),
)

Thanks to the version change above, your old schemas will now include zodiac_sign field but your new schemas will stay the same. Don't remove the zodiac business logic from your router because the old version will still need it. So you always return the zodiac sign but the schemas of the latest version will ignore it.

You can remove the logic for calculating and returning the zodiac sign after version 2000-01-01 gets deleted.

docs.title: Optional field
docs.text:
Let's say that we had a nullable middle_name field but we decided that it does not make sense anymore and want to remove it now from both requests and responses. This means that a user from an old version will still be able to pass it while the user from a new version will not. We can solve this by having this field in our HEAD, removing it from our latest version but keeping it in all older versions:

  1. Keep storing middle_name in your database in order to support old versions

  2. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01 to remove middle_name from the latest version:

    from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from users import BaseUser


class RemoveUserMiddleNameFromLatestVersion(VersionChange):
    """User requests and responses no longer include 'middle_name' because
    the product no longer uses it.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser).field("middle_name").didnt_exist,
    )

  3. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01 to leave support for middle_name in the older versions:

    from cadwyn import VersionChange, schema
from pydantic import Field
from users import BaseUser


class RemoveMiddleNameFromUser(VersionChange):
    """User requests and responses no longer include 'middle_name' because
    the product no longer uses it.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser)
        .field("middle_name")
        .existed_as(
            type=str | None,
            info=Field(description="User's Middle Name", default=None),
        ),
    )

  4. Add these migrations into the version bundle:

    # versions/__init__.py

from cadwyn import HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

from .v2001_01_01 import (
    RemoveMiddleNameFromUser,
    RemoveUserMiddleNameFromLatestVersion,
)

version_bundle = VersionBundle(
    HeadVersion(RemoveUserMiddleNameFromLatestVersion),
    Version("2001-01-01", RemoveMiddleNameFromUser),
    Version("2000-01-01"),
)

We added a new version with a breaking change but neither the HEAD schema that we use in business logic, neither has the business logic itself have changed one bit.

docs.title: Required field
docs.text:
There are two main cases with required fields:

  1. Remove a required field with a simple fake default (created_at)
  2. Remove a required field with an impossible default (tax id)

The first one is simple to solve: just use the approach above but use a default_factory=datetime.datetime.now instead of default=None. Add the same default_factory to the field in HEAD too: Cadwyn doesn't pass the defaults of older versions to HEAD (see the defaults warning), and the requests of the latest version don't have the field at all, so without a default in HEAD such requests fail.

Now what about case 2?

Let's say that you have company resources in your system. Let's also say that each company has a tax_id and now you would like to remove the tax_id field or make it optional. If tax_id was required in your responses, you can't really do this with traditional API versioning because you cannot come up with a sane non-null default for tax_id. It is a case of data versioning where you try to make an API version that is inconsistent with other API versions in terms of its data. You deal with this using one of the following approaches:

  1. Talk to your users. In any API versioning problem, talking to your users is the best first step. See whether this is actually a breaking change for them. Maybe only a small subset of your users is using this field and you can migrate this subset manually without much investment, which will allow you to make the breaking changes without breaking anyone's API. Though this approach becomes impossible to use once you get a lot of clients.
  2. Issue a warning to your users that tax_id is going to become optional in all API versions in N months and then make it so. This will allow you to avoid data versioning and your users will have a grace period to fix their issues. Then you can simply follow the approach above.
  3. Release a V2 version of your API which users will have to migrate their data to. This is a drastic approach and you should only reserve it for extreme cases but it is a correct way to represent data versioning.
  4. Disallow the new version (2001-01-01) to be used alongside older versions and disallow users to migrate to older versions after they have migrated to 2001-01-01. Then you can simply follow the approach above. This is a dirty hack and an inconvenience to your users but it solves the problem too, albeit I would never recommend to use this solition.

docs.title: Rename a field in schema
docs.text:
Assume you had a summary field before but now you want to rename it to bio.

  1. Rename the summary field to bio in users.BaseUser

  2. Add the following migration to versions.v2001_01_01:

    from cadwyn import (
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    VersionChange,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from users import BaseUser, UserCreateRequest, UserResource


class RenameUserSummaryToBio(VersionChange):
    """The user profile field 'summary' is now named 'bio' to match familiar
    profile terminology.
    """

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(BaseUser).field("bio").had(name="summary"),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(UserCreateRequest)
    def rename_summary_to_bio(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["bio"] = request.body.pop("summary")

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(UserResource)
    def rename_bio_to_summary(response: ResponseInfo):
        response.body["summary"] = response.body.pop("bio")

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Cadwyn is built around FastAPI and supports all of its functionality out of the box. One difference is that Cadwyn requires you to define API versions and extends your routing and Swagger to support API versioning.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text: uv add 'cadwyn[standard]'

docs.title: The basics
docs.text:
First, set up the most basic versioned app possible:

from cadwyn import Cadwyn, HeadVersion, Version, VersionBundle

app = Cadwyn(versions=VersionBundle(HeadVersion(), Version("2000-01-01")))


@app.get("/")
async def root():
    return {"message": "Hello World"}

and run it using:

fastapi dev main.py

That's it. That's the main difference between setting up FastAPI and Cadwyn: with Cadwyn you have to specify your API versions. Everything you specify at app level (such as using include_router or app.get(...)) will end up unversioned and essentially function like a regular FastAPI route.

docs.title: Docs
docs.text:
If you visit /docs, instead of the regular Swagger, you will see a version dashboard:

Clicking a card will take you to the card's regular Swagger page. If you wish to see the openapi.json for a specific version, use /openapi.json?version=2000-01-01 (or whatever version you want to get).

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text:
This tutorial provides steps for setting up automatic API versioning using Cadwyn. This will be illustrated with an example of a User API with changes to a User's address. The advanced version of the service from this tutorial is available here.

Adding a new API version in Cadwyn consists of two main steps:

  1. Make the breaking change
  2. Use Cadwyn to describe how to revert the breaking change

This tutorial will show how to prepare an environment for working with Cadwyn effectively in a basic usage example, how to make a breaking change, and how Cadwyn can help to keep the old API versions untouched.

docs.title: Step 0: Setting up
docs.text:
Here is an initial API setup where a User has a single address. The example implements two routes - one for creating a User and the other for retrieving User details. User ID is implemented as uuid.UUID. Please note that a dict is used in place of a database for simplicity but do not ever do it in real life.

The first API one comes up with usually doesn't require more than one address -- why bother?

import uuid

from cadwyn import (
    Cadwyn,
    Version,
    VersionBundle,
    VersionedAPIRouter,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserCreateRequest(BaseModel):
    address: str


class UserResource(BaseModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    address: str


database_parody = {}
router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.post("/users")
async def create_user(payload: UserCreateRequest) -> UserResource:
    id_ = uuid.uuid4()
    database_parody[id_] = UserResource(id=id_, address=payload.address)
    return database_parody[id_]


@router.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(user_id: uuid.UUID) -> UserResource:
    return database_parody[user_id]


app = Cadwyn(versions=VersionBundle(Version("2000-01-01")))
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

If you visit /docs, you will see the following dashboard:

The app is ready for use. To call its endpoints, pass X-API-VERSION header with value equal to 2000-01-01. But this is just one version. For a breaking change, Cadwyn supports multiple versioning styles, including header-based, path-based, and number-based.

docs.title: Step 1: Making the breaking change
docs.text:
Assume that during the development you realize that the initial API design is wrong and that address should be addresses so that the User can have several addresses to choose from. So now you want to change the type of the addresses field to a list of strings.

import uuid
from typing import Annotated

from cadwyn import (
    Cadwyn,
    Version,
    VersionBundle,
    VersionedAPIRouter,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class UserCreateRequest(BaseModel):
    addresses: list[str]


class UserResource(BaseModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    addresses: Annotated[list[str], Field(min_length=1)]


database_parody = {}
router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.post("/users")
async def create_user(payload: UserCreateRequest) -> UserResource:
    id_ = uuid.uuid4()
    database_parody[id_] = UserResource(id=id_, addresses=payload.addresses)
    return database_parody[id_]


@router.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(user_id: uuid.UUID) -> UserResource:
    return database_parody[user_id]


app = Cadwyn(versions=VersionBundle(Version("2001-01-01")))
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

Now your users will have their API integration broken. To prevent that, introduce API versioning. There aren't many methods of doing that. Most of them force you to either duplicate your schemas, your endpoints, or your entire app instance. And it makes sense, really: duplication is the only way to make sure that you will not break old versions with your new versions; the bigger the piece you are duplicating, the safer. Of course, the safest being duplicating the entire app instance and even having a separate database. But that is expensive and makes it either impossible to make breaking changes often or to support many versions. As a result, either you need infinite resources, very long development cycles, or your users need to migrate often from version to version.

Stripe has come up with a solution: to have one HEAD app version whose responses get migrated to older versions and to describe changes between these versions using migrations. This approach allows Stripe to keep versions for years without dropping them. Obviously, each breaking change still hurts and each version still makes the system more complex and expensive, but their approach gives you a chance to minimize this complexity. Additionally, it allows you to backport features and bugfixes to older versions. However, you will also be backporting bugs, which is a sad consequence of eliminating duplication.

Assume you need to know what your code looked like two weeks ago. You may use git checkout or git reset with an older commit because git stores the latest version of your code (which is also called HEAD) and the differences between it and each previous version as a chain of changes. This is exactly how Stripe's approach works. They store the latest version and use the diffs to regenerate the older versions.

Cadwyn is built upon this approach, so let's continue with the tutorial and combine the two versions that were created using versioning.

Note to curious readers Git doesn't actually work this way internally. The description above is closer to how SVN works. It's a simplistic metaphor to explain a concept.

docs.title: Step 2: Describing how to revert the breaking change
docs.text:
To fix the old integrations of your clients, you need to add back the 2000-01-01 version and its state. In Cadwyn, it is done using version changes (or, as Stripe calls them, version gates). You could also think of them as reverse database migrations (database migrations to downgrade to the previous state of the database). Essentially version changes describe the difference between the latest version and the previous version. They are a way to say "Okay, we have applied the breaking changes but here is how we would revert these changes for our old clients".

For every endpoint whose response_model is UserResource, this migration will convert the list of addresses back to a single address when migrating to the previous version. Your goal is to have an app of HEAD version and to describe what older versions looked like in comparison to it. That way the old versions are frozen in migrations and you can almost safely forget about them.

import uuid
from typing import Annotated

from cadwyn import (
    Cadwyn,
    RequestInfo,
    ResponseInfo,
    Version,
    VersionBundle,
    VersionChange,
    VersionedAPIRouter,
    convert_request_to_next_version_for,
    convert_response_to_previous_version_for,
    schema,
)
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class UserCreateRequest(BaseModel):
    addresses: list[str]


class UserResource(BaseModel):
    id: uuid.UUID
    addresses: Annotated[list[str], Field(min_length=1)]


database_parody = {}
router = VersionedAPIRouter()


@router.post("/users")
async def create_user(payload: UserCreateRequest) -> UserResource:
    id_ = uuid.uuid4()
    database_parody[id_] = UserResource(id=id_, addresses=payload.addresses)
    return database_parody[id_]


@router.get("/users/{user_id}")
async def get_user(user_id: uuid.UUID) -> UserResource:
    return database_parody[user_id]


class ReplaceUserAddressWithListOfAddresses(VersionChange):
    """Users can now store multiple addresses instead of a single address so they can choose among delivery locations."""

    instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version = (
        schema(UserCreateRequest)
        .field("addresses")
        .had(name="address", type=str),
        schema(UserResource).field("addresses").had(name="address", type=str),
    )

    @convert_request_to_next_version_for(UserCreateRequest)
    def change_address_to_multiple_items(request: RequestInfo):
        request.body["addresses"] = [request.body.pop("address")]

    @convert_response_to_previous_version_for(UserResource)
    def change_addresses_to_single_item(response: ResponseInfo) -> None:
        response.body["address"] = response.body.pop("addresses")[0]


app = Cadwyn(
    versions=VersionBundle(
        Version("2001-01-01", ReplaceUserAddressWithListOfAddresses),
        Version("2000-01-01"),
    )
)
app.generate_and_include_versioned_routers(router)

See how the first address is popped from the list? This is guaranteed to be possible if you specified earlier that min_length for addresses must be 1. If you didn't, then a user would be able to create a User in a newer version that would be impossible to represent in the older version. I.e. if anyone tried to get that user from the older version, they would get a ResponseValidationError because the user wouldn't have data for a mandatory address field. You need to always keep in mind that API versioning is only for versioning your API, your interface. Your versions must still be completely compatible in terms of data. If they are not, then you are versioning your data and you should go with a separate app instance. Otherwise, your users will have a hard time migrating back and forth between API versions and many unexpected errors.

Also note that the migration was added not only for the response but also for the request. This will allow your business logic to stay completely the same, no matter which version it was called from. Cadwyn will always give your business logic the request model from the HEAD version by wrapping each request in it.

Run the app and take a look at the generated dashboard and OpenAPI schemas:

The endpoint above is from the 2000-01-01 version. As you see, your routes and business logic are for the HEAD version but your OpenAPI has all the information about all the API versions which is the main goal of Cadwyn: a large number of long-living API versions without placing any burden on your business logic.

Obviously, this was just a simple example and Cadwyn has a lot more features so if you're interested -- take a look at the how-to and concepts sections.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page describes how Cadwyn works inside, at the level you need to change it. It doesn't repeat how to use Cadwyn: the concepts pages cover that. For why Cadwyn works this way and what it has already decided, read Design decisions and trade-offs.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
You write one version of the app: the latest one, called HEAD. Each older version is described only by how it differs from the next newer one, in version changes. From these, Cadwyn builds two things:

  1. Before the first request, it generates a copy of the models and the routes for every version.
  2. On every request, it validates the request with the routes of the client's version, migrates it up to HEAD, calls your HEAD endpoint, and migrates the response back down to the client's version.

So your business logic only ever sees HEAD, and every version's OpenAPI comes from real FastAPI routes.

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text: Module What it does cadwyn/structure/versions.py VersionChange, Version, HeadVersion, and VersionBundle. It also runs request and response migrations during a request (VersionBundle._versioned() and the methods it calls). cadwyn/structure/schemas.py, enums.py, endpoints.py The schema(), enum(), and endpoint() instructions. They only hold data: the generators apply them. cadwyn/structure/data.py RequestInfo, ResponseInfo, and the convert_request_to_next_version_for() and convert_response_to_previous_version_for() migrations. cadwyn/schema_generation.py Copies of models and enums for every version: generate_versioned_models() and SchemaGenerator. Also migrate_response_body(). cadwyn/route_generation.py Copies of routes for every version: generate_versioned_routers() and VersionedAPIRouter. cadwyn/applications.py Cadwyn, the FastAPI app. It wires everything together and serves the OpenAPI and docs pages of every version. cadwyn/middleware.py VersionPickingMiddleware and the version managers that read the version from a header or the path. cadwyn/routing.py _RootCadwynAPIRouter, which sends a request to the routes of its version. cadwyn/dependencies.py, cadwyn/_internal/context_vars.py current_dependency_solver() and the context variables behind it. cadwyn/__main__.py, _render.py, _asts.py The cadwyn render CLI, which prints a version's copies of models as code.

docs.title: Versions and version changes
docs.text:
A VersionBundle lists the versions from newest to oldest, optionally after a HeadVersion. VersionBundle.versions keeps that order, and VersionBundle.reversed_versions goes from oldest to newest. The oldest version can't have version changes, and each version change belongs to exactly one version.

The changes of a version describe how to turn that version into the previous, older one. When a VersionChange subclass is created, VersionChange.__init_subclass__() checks it and sorts its instructions by kind:

  • instructions_to_migrate_to_previous_version goes into alter_schema_instructions, alter_enum_instructions, and alter_endpoint_instructions.
  • The request and response migrations in the class body go into alter_request_by_schema_instructions, alter_request_by_path_instructions, alter_response_by_schema_instructions, and alter_response_by_path_instructions.

Schema generation and route generation read only these sorted attributes. See Version changes for how users write them.

docs.title: Schema generation
docs.text:
generate_versioned_models() in schema_generation.py returns a SchemaGenerator for every version:

  1. It wraps the models and enums that schema and enum instructions or request migrations by schema mention (VersionBundle.versioned_schemas and versioned_enums) into an editable description of the class: a _PydanticModelWrapper (fields, annotations, validators, and bases) or an _EnumWrapper (members). Other models are wrapped when they are first needed.
  2. It applies the HeadVersion instructions to these wrappers. Then it goes through the versions from newest to oldest. For each version, it saves a copy of the current wrappers in that version's SchemaGenerator, and then applies that version's schema and enum instructions so that the next, older version sees them.
  3. SchemaGenerator[Model] returns the version's copy of Model and creates it on first use. The copy is a new class built from the wrapper with the model's own metaclass. The models it refers to (in fields, bases, and so on) are replaced by their copies for the same version. The type args of generics, such as Item in Page[Item], are replaced only if they reach a model or enum with instructions, and some shapes keep the HEAD classes (see _should_version_generic_args() and the known limitations). The copy keeps a link to its HEAD model in __cadwyn_original_model__.

Cadwyn copies every model for every version, even models without instructions, because the copies differ from HEAD in small ways that older versions rely on, such as their OpenAPI names. The exceptions are enums and models in reference cycles whose copies would be the same as HEAD: enum members must stay the same objects, and a cycle can only be copied as a whole (_CycleCopier). SchemaGenerator._needs_copy() makes this decision. See Schema migrations, Enum migrations, and Schema generation for the user's side.

docs.title: Route generation
docs.text:
Cadwyn.generate_and_include_versioned_routers() only collects your routers. Cadwyn generates the routes before the first request, when the app gets its first ASGI call (Cadwyn._cadwyn_initialize()). It calls generate_versioned_routers() in route_generation.py, which works like schema generation, with a router instead of models:

  1. It copies your router once as the HEAD router. Cadwyn never serves the HEAD router directly. It keeps it to call your endpoints with HEAD data.
  2. It goes through the versions from newest to oldest with another copy of the router. For each version, it:
    1. replaces the models in the response models, dependencies, and endpoint signatures of every route with the version's copies from its SchemaGenerator, and rebuilds FastAPI's dependants for them;
    2. links the path-based request and response migrations of the version's changes to the matching HEAD routes;
    3. saves the router as the router of this version;
    4. copies it and applies the version's endpoint instructions to get the routes of the previous version. endpoint(...).didnt_exist tags a route as deleted instead of removing it, endpoint(...).existed removes the tag (routes marked with @router.only_exists_in_older_versions start tagged), and endpoint(...).had(...) changes the route's attributes.
  3. Because routes are only tagged and never removed during this loop, every route keeps its index in every copy. Cadwyn uses that index to find the HEAD route of each versioned route. It wraps the endpoint of every versioned route, including the routes of the newest version, with VersionBundle._versioned(), which holds both routes.
  4. Finally, it drops the routes tagged as deleted.

Cadwyn then adds each version's router to _RootCadwynAPIRouter.versioned_routers, with a dependency that documents the version header or path parameter in OpenAPI. Cadwyn.openapi_jsons() builds each version's OpenAPI from that version's routes. See Endpoint migrations for the user's side.

docs.title: The path of a request
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant M as VersionPickingMiddleware
    participant R as _RootCadwynAPIRouter
    participant F as FastAPI route of the client's version
    participant W as Cadwyn's endpoint wrapper
    participant E as Your HEAD endpoint
    C->>M: request with version 2000-01-01
    M->>R: store the version in api_version_var
    R->>F: pick the routes of 2000-01-01
    F->>W: validate with the 2000-01-01 models
    W->>W: migrate the request up to HEAD
    W->>W: validate again with the HEAD route
    W->>E: call with HEAD arguments
    E-->>W: HEAD response
    W->>W: migrate the response down to 2000-01-01
    W-->>F: response body
    F-->>C: serialize with the 2000-01-01 response model
  1. VersionPickingMiddleware reads the version with a HeaderVersionManager or a URLVersionManager, falls back to api_version_default_value, and stores the version in VersionBundle.api_version_var. It also returns the version that was used in the response header.
  2. _RootCadwynAPIRouter picks the routes: the unversioned routes if there's no version, the version's routes if it exists, or else, for date versions, the routes of the closest older version (waterfalling). If the middleware used the default version, the router tries the unversioned routes before that version's routes.
  3. The matched route is an ordinary FastAPI route of that version. FastAPI validates the request with the version's models and solves its dependencies, and then calls the route's endpoint, which is Cadwyn's wrapper.
  4. The wrapper turns the validated body back into data (or reads the raw body or form) and puts it in a RequestInfo. VersionBundle._migrate_request() runs the request migrations of every version newer than the client's, from oldest to newest. A body that is a container of models, such as list[Model], keeps the models of the client's version for the migrations. After the migrations, Cadwyn turns each of these models into the data of its set fields and extra keys, because FastAPI would read the models by their attributes (from_attributes=True) and lose their extra keys and set fields. It does so only where the body schemas of both the client's version and the latest version have models of the same class, through lists, dicts, and unions only, and only if every param of the latest version's dependencies that reads the body would validate it the same way and the app has no dependency overrides.
  5. It then solves the dependencies of the HEAD route with FastAPI's solve_dependencies(). This validates the migrated request with the HEAD models and runs the dependencies a second time (dependency re-execution). If this validation fails, a migration is wrong, so Cadwyn raises CadwynHeadRequestValidationError instead of returning a 422.
  6. It calls your endpoint with the HEAD arguments.
  7. It puts the result, or the HTTPException that the endpoint raised, in a ResponseInfo. VersionBundle._migrate_response() runs the response migrations of every version newer than the client's, from newest to oldest. It migrates error responses only if the migration sets migrate_http_errors=True.
  8. If the endpoint returned a body rather than a Response, FastAPI serializes the migrated body with the response model of the client's version.
  9. After the response and its background tasks, Cadwyn's root router drains FastAPI's file-cleanup stack under a cancellation shield bounded by the upload-close timeout. This protects files on Cadwyn's own unversioned routes and when a dependency fails before the versioned endpoint wrapper runs, while keeping the middleware's task boundaries and exception behavior. Standard disk-backed uploads close in daemon threads, so the deadline stops waiting even when synchronous filesystem I/O blocks, and a permanently blocked close cannot prevent process exit. Timed-out form streams are not retried by the outer upload collector. FastAPI then exits the already empty stack. Finally, Cadwyn.__call__ closes any uploads still open, including the ones that migrations put into the form, with its existing cancellation protection and per-upload timeout. Dependency teardown keeps FastAPI's own behavior.

Migrations by schema run only when the schema is the route's body or response model itself, or a member of a union that is. For a union, the wrapper picks the member that the validated body is (_get_union_member_of_body()), or the member whose model the endpoint returns an object of (_get_union_member_of_response()). _get_schema_migration_target() decides what a route's migrations are looked up by. Migrations by path run for the HEAD routes that route generation linked to them. See Data migrations for how users write migrations, and Costs of the architecture for what this design costs.

docs.title: Design decisions and trade-offs
docs.text: This page lists the trade-offs Cadwyn has accepted, its known limitations, and the rules for changing it. Read it before you propose a change to Cadwyn's behavior.

docs.title: Why most fixes are breaking changes
docs.text:
Cadwyn's output for an older API version is a public API. Clients of apps built on Cadwyn depend on it and can't opt out of a Cadwyn upgrade. Any change to what an older version accepts, returns, or documents in OpenAPI can break them, even when the old behavior was a bug. So Cadwyn treats the OpenAPI and behavior of every version as a frozen contract, and fixing long-standing bugs made 8.0.0 a major release.

The maintainer's principles follow from this:

  1. Existing users should almost never get breaking changes.
  2. FastAPI and Pydantic features should keep working transparently, but only as far as FastAPI and Pydantic themselves go.
  3. Every change should make Cadwyn simpler if possible. Complexity is the main long-term cost: after 8.0.0, schema_generation.py was about 4,000 lines and structure/versions.py about 2,000.

Cadwyn doesn't aim for "pay only for what you use". Prefer one behavior and one code path for every app over special paths that only some apps take, so bugs show up for everyone and get fixed once.

docs.title: Supported API
docs.text:
Everything importable from cadwyn is supported. So are these internals, which Airflow's Task SDK builds on. Changing them is a breaking change:

  • VersionBundle.versions and VersionBundle.reversed_versions
  • the alter_*_instructions attributes of VersionChange
  • calling the instructions in them (_AlterDataInstruction.__call__) with any object that has a body attribute
  • generate_versioned_models(), and indexing its result (SchemaGenerator.__getitem__ from cadwyn.schema_generation)

docs.title: Costs of the architecture
docs.text:
These follow from how Cadwyn works (see Architecture). They aren't bugs, and changes that try to remove them are almost always rejected.

  • Business logic sees only the latest version. Older versions are generated copies of the latest models, and migrations are written against the latest models.
  • Older versions use copies of the models and of changed enums. Identity checks (isinstance, is, dicts keyed by enum members) see these copies, e.g. in the first run of a versioned dependency. Objects that can't be deep-copied, such as a validator holding a threading.Lock, fail when their models are versioned.
  • Requests are validated twice: by their version's route, then, after migration, by the latest version's route. Dependencies run in both passes, so their side effects happen twice unless they check current_dependency_solver. Uploaded bytes files are held in memory twice. A model object that an endpoint returns is validated again against Cadwyn's copy of the response model, so its validators and model_post_init run twice, even with a single version (#592). Skipping that would also skip the coercion of objects built with model_construct() or model_copy(update=...), and change the responses of apps that rely on it.
  • Migrations run only for the schema you name: the route's body or response_model, or a member of a union that is (for the requests and responses that are that member). They don't run for that schema nested in other schemas or generics. Schema instructions change a schema everywhere it's used. This way each migration runs once, where it was declared.
  • Cadwyn relies on FastAPI, Pydantic, and typing internals, such as solve_dependencies, fastapi._compat, FastAPI's lazily included routers, FieldInfo internals, and typing's alias cache, so upstream minor releases can break it. The twice-daily workflow upgrades every dependency and runs the tests to catch this. It must always pass. Fix failures in Cadwyn, never by pinning or capping a dependency.
  • Startup copies every model for every version. Copying only the changed models would be much faster, but it would change OpenAPI names and model behavior, so it isn't planned.

docs.title: Decisions already made
docs.text: Area Decision Why Generic models (Page[Item]) Their type args are always versioned, with no option to turn it off. User-reported bug (#416). Options double the test matrix and the code paths. Inherited fields schema(Child).field(...) changes only Child and its subclasses. User-reported bug (#466). Renaming a field in a subclass while a base still has it Fails at startup, naming the base. Rename the field where it's declared, and in the same version in subclasses that changed it in newer versions. The subclass had both fields, because Pydantic models can't drop inherited fields. Not inheriting from the parent's copy would break the parent's validators and isinstance (#525). Renaming a field in a parent while a subclass declares it, changed it in a newer version, or gets it from another base Fails at startup, naming the subclass. Rename it in the subclass or the other base too, in the same version. The subclass had both fields. Renaming it automatically would break apps that already rename it in both, and would guess when other bases have the new name (#581). didnt_exist for a field that a subclass declares again or changed, while a base still has it Fails at startup, naming the base. Delete it from the base in the same version. The instruction did nothing, without an error, because the subclass still inherited the base's field (#582). Annotated[T, Depends(f)] Versioned only in the versions that change the models or enums that f validates. Versioning it everywhere exposed copies to identity checks (#467). Missing an exotic case, such as a recursive type alias, keeps the previous behavior, which is acceptable. Converters of union members (Union[A, B], Optional[A]) Since 9.0, they run for the member that the client's version validated, or whose model the endpoint returned. If Cadwyn can't tell the member, it fails. A migration of the whole union replaces its members' migrations in the same version change. User-reported bug (#530). Before 9.0, they never ran for unions. Running one member's migration on another's data would corrupt values. Validating responses to find the member would run their validators twice, since FastAPI validates them after the migrations. Converters inside nested models Won't do. Write the converter for the outer schema. Running nested converters by default would convert data twice in apps that already follow the docs (#468). Computed fields that return versioned models Documented limitation. Expose the data as a regular field. Every Pydantic serializer that picks a model by the value's type loses nested JSON config, changes duck-typed values, or re-wraps user exceptions (#469). .had(alias=...) and .didnt_have("alias") Since 9.0, they also change the validation and serialization aliases that Pydantic derived from alias, as Field() does, so the wire key matches the documented one. Data with only the old key fails (a 422 or a 500) instead of getting the field's default. 8.x only warned at startup. Clients of apps without migrations relied on the old key, so the fix waited for a major release and must fail loudly instead of losing their values (#465). Fields whose validation and serialization keys differ Fix only the requests and responses that would certainly fail ("rescue-only"). Responses that passed before must not change, even if they lost a value. Self-referencing models Copied when that's safe. Otherwise, Cadwyn raises SchemaGenerationError at startup. A clear failure is better than serving wrong shapes. Enum defaults of omitted parameters on FastAPI before 0.148 Not rewritten. It would fix a pre-existing bug on old FastAPI only, and every attempt added new edge cases. /changelog, generate_changelog(), and hidden() Removed in 9.0. Maintenance cost. Apps can generate a better changelog from their version changes themselves, e.g. with a coding agent. Options and flags Avoided in 99% of cases, and added only with the maintainer's sign-off. A breaking fix doesn't get one to ship early: it waits for a major release. Each one doubles the code paths and the tests. Minimum supported versions Raising the FastAPI minimum to drop compatibility code is fine. The Pydantic and Python minimums are raised only when unavoidable. FastAPI moves fast, and Cadwyn depends on its internals. Raising the Pydantic or Python minimum blocks more users. FastAPI before 0.137.1 Not supported. Its router model is different. Supporting both doubles the routing code.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
These are accepted for now. Fixing one is a separate change with its own issue.

  • TypeVars used only in typed extra fields (__pydantic_extra__ with extra="allow") aren't versioned reliably, especially in nested generics, so older versions can validate and document their latest bounds, constraints, or defaults. Use a concrete annotation such as __pydantic_extra__: dict[str, Item] on a non-generic model (#584).
  • Generic models keep the latest models in older versions when a type arg refers back to its own model through a quoted annotation, such as Optional[Page["Category"]] in Category, or uses a recursive native type alias. A PEP 695 generic model that refers to itself through a quoted annotation, such as nxt: Optional["Wrap[X]"] in class Wrap[X](BaseModel), returns a 500 in every version instead of failing at startup. On Pydantic 2.14.2 and newer, this happens only when a version change alters its type arg.
  • Recursive native type aliases work only if they contain nothing but builtin types (including Union and Literal) and other such aliases, like type JsonData = dict[str, JsonData] | list[JsonData] | str | int | None. A route that uses one with anything else in it, such as a model, an enum, a forward ref, or Annotated, fails with a SchemaGenerationError that names the alias when Cadwyn generates the route. Models in a reference cycle (e.g. children: "list[Category]" in Category) that use such an alias fail with a SchemaGenerationError if any version has schema or enum instructions.
  • Enum copies unwrap enum-valued members, including values passed to had(). For Outer.a = Inner.a, the copy's value is Inner.a.value, and members with equal raw values can become aliases. Changing this would change existing requests, responses, validation errors, and OpenAPI. Define versioned enums with raw values (see Enum migrations).
  • A request with a plain Enum or Flag that has enum(...) instructions returns a 500 if Cadwyn can't convert its members to the latest enum. Cadwyn converts them in standard containers and in plain lazy fields such as Iterable[Kind]. It doesn't convert them in models it doesn't dump (e.g. a top-level Iterable[Item] body), in your own containers or iterators, in embedded bodies, with dependency overrides, or in lazy fields with alternative union branches, Any, opaque validators, complex validation aliases, or enums with custom lookup, equality, or non-primitive values.
  • A strict response model (e.g. ConfigDict(strict=True)) with a plain Enum or Flag that has enum(...) instructions returns a 500 in every version, including the latest. This includes optional fields and nested models or containers. Add Field(strict=False) to the enum field. In older versions, a response migration that supplies that version's enum members also works (see Enum migrations). A fix would change the enum's schema and what custom schema hooks see.
  • Schema instructions:
    • Diamond inheritance takes the field from the first base, as Pydantic does.
    • A parent's rename reaches a subclass's own changes only through single, non-generic inheritance.
    • A parent's rename of x to y leaves both x and y, without a startup error, in a subclass that declares x again, if a class between them changed x in a newer version and deletes it in the version of the rename. For example, schema(Middle).field("x").had(description=...), then schema(Parent).field("x").had(name="y") and schema(Middle).field("x").didnt_exist with class Child(Middle) declaring x.
    • had(default=PydanticUndefined) doesn't make a field required when its default is declared in Annotated[..., Field(default=...)].
    • didnt_have(...) raises an AttributeError when the attribute is a read-only property of an Annotated metadata object.
    • schema(Model).validator(...).existed for a computed field fails on Python before 3.13.
  • Alias instructions decide from the incoming data whether it has only a field's old key (see .had(alias=...) in Decisions already made). So the renamed_key error happens even when a model validator would fill the field from other keys, e.g. a model_validator(mode="before") that copies a compatibility_name key into it.
  • Defaults: Cadwyn swaps in the version's model classes, enum classes, and functions only inside the lists, tuples, and dicts in defaults and other field attributes (see Defaults). Elsewhere, they stay the latest ones: e.g. in sets, deques, MappingProxyType, a defaultdict's default_factory, dataclass and model instances, or functools.partial args. Each version gets a copy.deepcopy() of subclasses of list, tuple, and dict, and of containers that contain themselves. So a custom __deepcopy__ or __reduce__ decides what versions share (one that returns self shares the whole default), a sentinel inside is a different object in every version, Counter loses its attributes, and some cycles through tuples lose identity.
  • cadwyn render renders model_config only for models whose config a version changes, and omits it for the rest. It renders AliasChoices and AliasPath as calls that raise a TypeError, and subclasses of scalars such as int and str as the base type. It raises CadwynRenderError for defaults it can't reproduce, such as recursive or shared mutable defaults, subclasses whose repr looks like a builtin container, or a defaultdict with a lambda factory. Use a named Field(default_factory=...) function for these (see Rendering schemas). Other subclasses render through their constructor and __repr__, which must reproduce their contents and state.
  • Class dependencies (except Pydantic models) aren't versioned.
  • WebSocket routes select the API version and support existence, path, name, and dependency instructions, but Cadwyn doesn't migrate their schemas or messages.
  • Streaming (generator or server-sent-event) endpoints don't work in versioned routes.
  • Request bodies that are lists or dicts of models (e.g. list[Model]) pass the client's extra keys and set fields to the latest version only when Cadwyn can be sure they're right (#566). Roughly, both versions must have the same fields, keys, and defaults at the same place, directly in lists, dicts, or unions, with no validators that get the raw input (e.g. model_validator(mode="before")) and no custom __init__. Every latest-version param that reads the body must validate it the same way. Models in tuples, sets, or deques, root models, and all bodies in apps with app.dependency_overrides never qualify. Other models are read by their attributes, as before: they lose their extra keys, and all their fields count as set. A required field whose alias differs from its name returns a 500. An optional one whose model doesn't validate its serialization alias (e.g. Field(default=0, alias="x", validation_alias="v")) gets its default without an error.
  • Request body models that override model_dump() (e.g. SQLModel models) still pass their computed fields to the latest version as input: as extra keys, or as a 500 if the model forbids extra keys. Cadwyn can't tell whether an override accepts exclude_computed_fields (SQLModel before 0.0.26 doesn't), so it calls it as before (#570).
  • Json[...] fields of request bodies (#538): Cadwyn encodes their values for the latest version only when it can be sure that the latest version gets what the client sent. Otherwise, the latest version parses the already parsed values again. A value that isn't a string then returns a 500 in every version, unless a migration encoded it as a JSON string. Json[str] returns a 500 or another string. Json[Any] and other types that accept several JSON types give the endpoint another value, e.g. 123 instead of "123". Cadwyn encodes only the strings that the client sent and that are still at their place, including in copies made with dict() or copy.deepcopy(). It passes values as they are when:
    • a migration set the value as a string, or the value doesn't survive a JSON round trip (e.g. an empty string, null, a tuple, a NaN, or a dict with mixed key types). Cadwyn still encodes the client's other strings. One exception: if a migration interns the client's string with sys.intern() and puts equal interned JSON at the same place, Python returns the client's string object. Cadwyn then encodes it, and the endpoint gets a string instead of the parsed JSON.
    • a migration moved or removed a client's string (e.g. by reordering a list), replaced a list, dict, or model with another type, or put keys other than strings, numbers, booleans, and null in a dict on the way to the field
    • the body differs between the request's version and the latest one, or a latest-version dependency reads it as another type (e.g. body: dict = Body())
    • the body's schema isn't plain JSON, e.g. it has validators, serializers, model_post_init, computed fields, default factories other than builtin containers (e.g. Field(default_factory=lambda: 1) next to a Json[...] field returns a 500), unions with non-JSON members (e.g. models or dates), models that allow extra keys or dump to other keys, or Json[...] fields in tuples, in self-referencing models, or more than 8 models deep
    • the request has no body, or, on FastAPI 0.158.2 and newer, a migration sets the body of an omitted optional form model
    • the field is in a list or dict body that falls back (see above), or has a string value there
    • a request migration runs and the field has a string that Python shares, such as "" or some one-character strings (e.g. "5" with some pydantic-core versions, which becomes 5)
  • Unions of form models on FastAPI 0.153.0 and newer: Cadwyn can't pass a list, set, or tuple from a validator or a migration whole to every member when one member takes that field as a single value (e.g. value: Any) and another as repeated values (e.g. value: list[str]) or as an extra field. On FastAPI 0.153.0 to 0.160.x, the body passes as it is, like in Cadwyn 8.x: a single-value field gets only the last item, and a repeated-values field gets a set or tuple as one item. If that member accepts the body, the endpoint gets a wrong value without an error, e.g. ["b"] instead of ["a", "b"]. On FastAPI 0.161.0 and newer, the request fails with a CadwynError that names the field and the members, as it does when a form model outside the union (e.g. of a dependency override) shares the body and would get a list in a list.
  • Form models on FastAPI 0.158.2 and newer: FastAPI reads a form model and the other form params of the endpoint, its dependencies, and their overrides from one dict body. Cadwyn gives each param what FastAPI would give it for the migrated request, e.g. an int where the form had a string, if a migration set one.
    • If Cadwyn can't, the request fails with a CadwynError (a 500): when a param takes the whole body (e.g. payload: dict = Body() in an override), when another param uses the alias of an endpoint's form model that a dependency declares, or, after a migration, when a param reads a key that the form model took under another name (e.g. through AliasChoices) or the model's migrated body isn't a dict, and when a migration sets a key to a dict or a collection in a collection while an optional form model is omitted, since a form can't hold it. Use distinct names or aliases, or read the form from Request.
    • If an optional form model was omitted and nothing else reads the form, a migrated key named like the model param counts as the embedded model. For body: Annotated[Optional[MyModel], Form()] = None whose model has a body: str field, request.body = {"body": "value"} fails. Set request.body = {"body": {"body": "value"}}.
  • On Cadwyn's routes, uploaded files keep closing after the client disconnects, but Cadwyn waits only three seconds. Slower uploads are still open when the request ends. Disk files finish closing in daemon threads, which don't block process exit. Your own close overrides and in-memory files keep FastAPI's behavior. Mounted non-Cadwyn apps and versioned routers in plain FastAPI apps keep their host app's cleanup.

docs.title: Rules for changing Cadwyn
docs.text:
Scope

  • Fix the reported bug, not its neighbors.
  • File the bugs you find yourself as issues. Fix them only if a user reported them or they crash.
  • Don't add unsupported features as part of a fix, such as migrations of WebSocket messages, streaming endpoints, StreamingResponse, or FileResponse.
  • Don't widen a change during review. If a review uncovers a new problem, file it.
  • If user code has a simple workaround and the fix in Cadwyn is complex, document the workaround instead.
  • Rank review findings by how likely they are in real apps. A contrived case that breaks working output still gets fixed, but it shouldn't drive the design.
  • Decide which breaking changes a major release takes when the work starts, not in the audit before the release. 8.0.0 rolled back and redesigned two fixes late (#457 and #475, #458 and #474).

What a change may alter

  • Compare every change against the last release, not against an idea of correct behavior.
  • A change may alter output that is broken today: a crash, a 500, an empty or lost value. It may not alter output that works today, even if it's wrong, unless the maintainer accepts it as a breaking change with an upgrade note in the CHANGELOG.
  • The OpenAPI of every version counts as output, including schema names.
  • When clients rely on behavior that differs from the docs, a fix toward the docs is a breaking change. Warn at startup in the current major version, naming the model, the field, and how to keep working, and change the behavior in the next one.

How to fix

  • Prefer doing less. Narrow the fix, apply it only when the old path fails ("retry on failure", not an extra validation pass), or go back to the last release's code path.
  • If every review round finds new edge cases in the same part of a fix, remove that part instead of patching it again.
  • Don't reimplement FastAPI, Pydantic, or CPython logic. Call their functions, and evaluate annotations only where FastAPI itself does.
  • Make safety checks allow-lists. Anything unknown takes the old behavior.
  • Decide statically, not by the order in which models happen to be generated.
  • Find what needs versioning and copy it in one traversal, never two that must agree. Finding must not copy, wrap, or rebuild unchanged models.
  • Keep the user's objects as they are, and copy only what FastAPI or Pydantic would mutate. deepcopy doesn't isolate things: it goes through typing's caches and breaks objects compared with is, such as FastAPI's sentinels.
  • Caches may share structure between models or versions, but never user-visible state such as a stateful default factory.
  • Invalid instructions or models fail at startup with an error that names the model and the field. Never fail later at request time, and never serve wrong data without an error.
  • When you rely on a private FastAPI or Pydantic internal, check at import time that it exists, and fail with a clear error if it changed instead of falling back.
  • Cadwyn() accepts FastAPI's parameters and passes each of them to every router it creates.
  • In the user docs, describe the common case and its workaround. The full list of shapes that a rule covers belongs in the tests.

How to check a change

  • Compare the requests and the OpenAPI of every version against the last release, installed in its own checkout or virtual environment.
  • Run the tests on the minimum supported and the latest Pydantic, and on Python 3.11 and 3.14. Check CI on every operating system before merging: recursion and stack limits differ on Windows and macOS.
  • Pytest puts the root of the checkout it runs from first on sys.path, so run a test file from the checkout that you want to test.
  • After merging main into a branch, look for top-level functions that are now defined twice. The later definition wins without a warning.

docs.title: How to build a versioning framework
Questions to consider when evaluating your framework
How simple is it to create a new API version?
docs.text: If it is too simple, it is probably a trap. The framework is probably hiding too much complexity from you. For example, early on the Cadwyn dev team tried a straightforward "copy the entire business logic into a separate directory" approach which made it so easy to add new versions. We added too many of them in the end, thus it got hellishly hard to maintain or get rid of those versions.

docs.title: How simple is it to delete an old API version?
docs.text: Your framework should allow you to clean up versions as simply and cheaply as possible. For example, if your framework tries to minimize the amount of code duplication in your repository by new routes including old routes and by new business logic inheriting from classes from old business logic, then deleting an old version is going to be painful (often even dangerous) as versions can quickly start interacting with each other turning a single small application into a set of interconnected applications.

docs.title: How simple is it to see the differences between API versions?
docs.text: The simpler it is, the better off your users are.

docs.title: What exactly do you need to duplicate in order to create a new API version?
docs.text: The less you duplicate and maintain manually, the simpler it is to support. However, the less you duplicate, the greater the risk of breaking older versions in subsequent releases.

docs.title: How simple is it to detect accidental data versioning?
docs.text: Data versioning is an important issue when versioning your API. If your framework makes it hard to version data -- it's really good!

docs.title: How we got here
